STANLEYLYALLCHANNON
Our Grand Master is a transplanted Australian, and everyone could recognize that fact with the fust words he spoke after being installed as the Grand
Master of Masons in California, when he greeted the audience with the typical
Australian expression, "G'Day, Mate". H e was born in Bendigo, Victoria,
Australia, on March 25, 1924, where his father and grandfather were both
Masons. He is the fust Australian, and the first to have been born in the
Southern Hemisphere, to become the Grand Master in California. His ready
wit has been displayed on many occasions throughout the State when an
unexpected incident wouJd trigger his immediate response.
At the age of 15, he was awarded a competitive Government scholarship at
the University of Melbowne in Victoria, Australia, and graduated in 1944 with
the degree of Bachelor of Metallurgical Engineering. Following a period of
service with the Ministry of Munitions, Defense D epartment in Australia, be
was awarded a Research Fellowship at the University of Utah. There, he
furthered his education by earning a Master o f Science Degree in Metallurgical
Engineering in 1948. He completed his formal education in 1951, when he was
the second person to receive the Degree of Doctor of Philosophy, Metallurgical
Engineering, at the University of Illinois.
After graduation from Illinois, he joined the DuPont Company to do
research on titanium, and later moved to Spokane, Washington, where he
developed new aluminum alloys for Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corporation. Many of these new alloys are now used extensively in commerce and m the
d efense industries. H e moved to Riverside, California in October 1955 to
become a Research Metallurgist with Hunter Engineering Company, where he
assisted in the d evelopment of continuous casting and fabrication of aluminum
products. H e has also served as Chief, T echnical Staff of Rohr Corporation,
and later as Manager, Materials Staff, The Aerospace Corporation. Following
his retirement in 1979, J:ie was requested by the Government to conduct a special
study for the Department of Defense in Washington, D.C. Upon returnmg to
Riverside, he continued his work as a Private Consultant on Materials Technology, as well as continuing as a Consultant to the Institute fo r D efense Analysis,
Washington, D.C. He is a member of the American Society for Metals, the
Society for the Advancement of Materials and Process Engmeering, and the
Institute for Metals.
Brother Channon met and married Elizabeth (Beth) CaJlaway on July 20,
1949 in Tuscola, Illinois. They have one daughter, Nancy, a Past Honored Queen
of Bethel No. 340, International Order of Job's Daughters, and two sons, John
and Bryan. They are also the pro ud grandparents to two lovely SU.-ls. Stan and
Beth are members of Calvary Presbytenan Chwch o f Riverside. Stan was
involved in Scouting at an early age and earned the rank of King's Scout in
Australia. He became a Cubmasler for three years, and a Scoutmaster of Troop
112 for five years in the United Stales while his two sons were active. He has
continued to be interested and active in out-door activities such as hikin~
backpacking, water skiing, boating (he has his own boat) and flying. Stan 1s
licensed as a private pilot and a member of a Flying Club. He often flies to

The Grand Jurisdiction of California has been blessed to have had the
benefit of the engineering training and the analytical mind of Most Worshipful
Stan, to lead our Grand Lodge and the Masons of California, through some very
trying events this year.

Brother Channon was raised in Evergreen Lodge No. 259, Riverside, on
September 19, 1959 and his first office was as Chaplain in 1961. He beeame
Master of Evergreen Lodge in 1965. He served on the Grand Lodge Correspondence Committee (1963-1965) and on June 21, 1966 was appointed Inspector
of the 616th Masonic District, an office he held with distinct10n until September
1978, when he was called to Washington, D.C. He was very active in the
administration of Evergreen Lodge, being Chairman of the Building Committee
from 1969 to 1976, when the new Chica~o Avenue Temple was constructed. He
was the driving force behind the design and construction of this beautiful
Temple. He was President of the Evergreen Temple Association and a member
of the Board of Trustees from 1976 to 1978. He served on the Board of Trustees,
Masonic Homes of California from 1983 until he was installed as Grand Master.
He has been outstanding as a Trustee, being one of their most innovative
members. His work can be seen in the new Siminoff Center and Lorber Medical
Services Building at the Union City Masonic Home, and in the new Adult
Apartment Units at the Covina Home, both of which he had the privilege of
dedicating during his year as Grand Master. He was elected to the Office of
Junior Grand Warden in October 1985 and progressed through the Grand
Lodge Line to be installed as the 124th Grand Master of Masons in California ·
and Hawaii on October 12, 1988.
Most Worshipful Channon has han another first--the first Grand Master of
California to lose part of his J urisdiction--when the Brethren of Hawaii formed
their own Grand Lodge in May 1989. However, he had the privilege oflnstalling
the Officers of the Grand Lodge of Hawaii on July 1, 1989 in Honolulu. He was
also privileged to take part in the Centenary Celebration and Installation of the
United Grand Lodge of Victoria, Australia in March 1989, being one of their
principal speakers.
Most Worshipful Channon is a Past President of the Southern California
Past Masters Association. He holds membership in the Valley of Long Beach
Scottish Rite, and was honored with the Rank and Decoration of Knight
Commander of the Court of Honor, in December 1985. He is a member of the
Riverside York Rite Bodies; Riverside Chapter No. 67, Royal Arch Masons;
Riverside Council No. 59, Cryptic Masons; and Riverside Commandcry No. 28,
Knights Templar. He is a member of Rive.rside High-Twelve Club, St. Gabriel
Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine, Al Malaikah Sh.rine Temple, the
Roayl Order of Scotland, The Robert Bruce Association, National Sojourners,
and an Honorary DeMolay. He holds Honorary Membership in several other
Masonic Organizations.
The theme for his year as Grand Master has been "Accent On Youth" which
has been expressed on lapel buttons using that theme with the Square and
Compass, and also that theme with a Kangaroo on a button for the Ladies and
Youth. He also had pins in the shape of a Koala for both the Masons and the
Ladies. Most Worshipful Channon has taken every opportunity this year to
speak to the youth, and to reach out to them with assistance by enlarging the
Grand Lodge Youth Orders Committee.

As manv of you know, I love golf. One day I met a stranger on a public goU
course and we played a round of ~olf. When we were finished, I complimented
him on his game. "Well," he said, "it's not as good as it used to be. I'm just getting
into my game again. I just returned from three years in the mission field in
Africa, and they didn't have golf where we were." "Are you a minister?" I asked.
"No." "A doctor?" "No." "A dentist?" "No." "Then what are you?" "I'm a carpenter." "What did you do?" "I built an infirmary, a small hangar for the mission
airplane, a couple of small houses, and converted two old buildings into a
school." This is his story; "I've always loved my God. I've always prayed, 'use me
as You will, but after all, I'm only a bumble carpenter.' One night I was serving
refreshments at the men's mec:ting when [ got a phone call from the mission
Board asking me to take my wife and two children to Africa for three years. My
wife and I prayed about it, and we decided it was either put up or shut up. So
we went."

The peasant wanted the blessing, but not the responsibility. The carpenter
said, "either put up, or shut up."
My Brethren, recall the words of the Master of your Lodge on the occasion
of your being raised as a Master Mason: "The eyes of the Fraternity are now
upon you; be just, be faithfu~ be true and convince the world, by your acts, that
on becoming a Master Mason you have become a better man." That is no idle
tale as told by an idiot! That is the calling of every man who wears the Lamb
Skin! That "Congratulation" by the Master goes on to have you sign the by-laws
and he instructs you, "Which will subject you to its burdens and its responsibilities, as well as entitle you to its benefits and its privileges." I don't know
whether your hearing aid is turned on or not, whether you are asleep or awake,
but hear me out. At that point in your Masonic life you were told the benefits,
the privileges and the responsibilities of being a Master Mason, and you were
told, in essence, either put up, or shut up.
Our world is vastly different from what it used to be. You know, "The good
old days." Those days that we "remember" but probably never really were. We
can easily be lulled into an euphoric dream of what used to be. We may even be
tempted to go back. As one Master Mason to another, I say to you, AWAKE,
STAND UP AND PARTIC IPATE IN A NEW FUTURE! Almighty God
never leads backward! Yes, our world has changed, and it is still changin$. This
is the 140th Communication of the Grand Lodge of California. At the ume of
its founding in 1850, there were only a few Masons and but three Lodges. Times
have changed! There was no magnificent building for its meetings such as this
were we are assembled. Times have changed! Yet the ideals of those early
California Masons were so very similar to ours of today. Let me give you an
example. The first business of that April, 1850 meeting was to grant a charter
under the name of Berryman Lodge No. 4 in Sacramento. The name was
changed to Jennings Lodge No. 4. By May, 1853, Jennings Lodge had surrendered its charter. Why? Because that Lodge was, and I quote from its
minutes, "Burdened with a debt of $14,000 not contracted by the present
members of the Lodge, but by Masonic Fraternity in general." Earlier, a report
by the Grand Lecturer indicated this deht was from "the extension of charity to
Brethren not members of the [Jennings] Lodge." Those Brethren sacrificed
their Lodge in giving relief to needy Brother Masons. Times have changed!
Earthquakes have brought down, and fires have consumed. Wars have been
fought, and peace bas been waged. Airplanes have been flown, and our satellites

9

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

are now penetrating uncharted space. Inner-city ghettos and ghetto blasters are
here to stay. The change is staggering! Both for good and for bad. Today
intentional improvements for the good, even among Masons, require very hard
work that must be sustained by a deep caring about the needs of those facing a
life plagued with hunger, malnutrition, joblessness, drugs, alcohol, and gang
violence. Just within the past few months I heard an account of how life really
is on the streets. The leader of a Community Center in Seattle announced,
"Don't you realize that the gangs of our cities in America are to the crime
syndicate what the Junior Achievement Program is to corporate America!" That
is one reason I am so thankful that the Grand Lodge of California is hard at
work with its Substance Abuse Program. I'm sure we will all awee that what we
are now doing is not near enough, but we are doing something. Too long we
Masons have been sitting on the sidelines, with our heads (and minds) hidden
in a hole in the ground as ostrich-like dreamers! Awake and stand up and
participate in a new future. Let the people of our land know that we care! The
only things to hold us back are the limitless confinements we place on ourselves.

and distinctive way. But it needs to be done. It's not what you say, it's what you
do that counts. Words need never be spoken. Just become a part of the action!
Put on that square and compass and convince the world, by what you do, that
you have become a better man. That's Masonry at work. That's participating in
a new future.

My text comes from the Judeo-Christian heritage, althou~h it can also be
found, in principle, in almost all of the world's Holy Writings: ' Choose you this
day whom ye will serve. And Joshua said unto the people, ye are witnesses
against yourselves that ye have chosen the Lord, to serve him. And they said,
we are witnesses." Remember what the Master of your Lodge said. "Convince
the world, by your acts, that on becoming a Master Mason you have become a
better man." There were witnesses to the Master making that statement to you.
You are witnesses as well, for you wear the badge of a Mason attesting to that
event.
On January 26th of this year, the Grand Lodge held a Cornerstone
Ceremony for the county jail in Sacramento. It was a beautiful day, a beautiful
ceremony1 and a beautiful building. But the statement of one of the planners of
that buildmg almost ruined the whole day when he told me, "There is nothing
as expensive as building a prison for a little boy... in a certain neighborhood ...at
the age of ten years ...so that we can take care of him when he is old enough to
be sent here for crimes he will have committed." The statement was so profound
that I hurried to write it down. Then I asked for an explanation. He said, "We
know he will be here but the problem is others will have already taken his place."
Wake up, Brethren, participate in a new future. The vision for our future can
~ as beautiful, as full and enjoyable as is our participation in changing the
direction of our resources, giving of our time, risking, modeling, molding,
shap~g, caring, listening, supporting, even helping. There are concrete ways of
changing the path of life around us. We should take hold of our visions, one by
one, and then commit all our strength and energy to see them fulfilled.
We hear much criticism of our Fraternity these days. Many people assail
us from every side. I hear their remarks and so do you. As I have listened to
fellow clergymen during the past several years, I must admit that there is one
substantial reason for their campaign to smear all that Freemasonry stands for.
They are jealous...jealous for our time and commitment. Because of our obvious
apathy - even total disregard - toward recognized religious practices, we appear
to have deflated our spiritual values by eliminating our participation at our
chosen house of worship. But you and I, as Master Masons, know that we have
not deflated our spiritual values. So we would do well to overcome this erroneous thinking. This is a job for individual Masons. Each in his own unique

In the early days of railroading, a man decided to take his first train ride on
a visit to a neighboring town. He boarded the one-coach train and seated himself
on a hard wooden seat. "First class, second class, or third class?" asked the
conductor. He had no idea what the conductor was talking about, so he asked,
"Which is cheapest?" "Third class," answered the conductor after marking a "3"
on the back of his ticket. The man was bewildered as he watched the other
passengers buying a mixture of the three tickets. His questions were answered,
however, when the small steam engine came to a shuddering halt on a steep
grade. "First class passengers, keep your seats!" yelled the conductor. "Second
class passengers, get out and walk! Third class passengers, get out and push!" I
have the feeling that we Masons should all have "Third class tickets", and get
out there and push as hard as we possibly can on behalf of Freemasonry.
I believe it was the lawyer, Clarence Darrow, who said "I don't fmish, I stop."
I'm not really finished, but I am going to stop. Brethren, perhaps you are like
the peasant who wanted the good things in life without any of the responsibilities. Maybe you can grasp the meaning of the term commitment as did the
carpenter. Or, by chance you are able to identify with the third class passenger
who learned that things only happened through his own efforts. Well, to all of
you, my Brethren, I say awake, stand up and participate in a new future.

NECROLOGY REPORT
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:

It is appropriate and proper that we pause for a few moments early in this
140th Annual Communication to pay our respect to the memory of our departed
Brethren. We are reminded of that passage in our ritual - "Man that is born of
a woman is of few days and full of trouble, he cometh forth as a flower and is
cut down. He fleeth also as a shadow and c.ontinueth not." Man comes and
cultivates the soil and in the end lies beneath it. This brief sentence totals up the
life and death of us mortals. All of us who are in attendance here today know
"that a time will come for each of us and the wisest know not how soon when all
distinction but that of goodness shall cease and Death the mighty leveler of us
all will reduce us to the same state." Freemasonry is a fraternal society and we
cannot remain neutral for we are engaged in a moral and spiritual battle for the
survival of freedom, justice and unwavering virtues. We must maintain the
standards of integrity, brotherly love, relief and truth so essentially necessary in
this modern age. It is for Freemasonry to discover that which we must never
surrender - belief in a Supreme Bein~. All of the worlds messiahs have sought
to unify the spiritual and earthly qualities of man, providing a model of perfection. This is the perfection taught in Masonry.
Your Committee wishes it might be possible to include even a brief statement regarding the accomplishments of these Brethren who have so freely and
unselfishly given of their time to promote that spirit of amity and goodwill which

should characterize those who bear the title of Mason. Since we last met, this
Grand Lodge has lost a total of 545 Past Masters, .Masters and .Wardens

country from whose bourne no traveller returns. Their i!ldi~dual names will be
inscribed in the printed record of our Annual Commumcauon. And so we take
leave of our departed Brethren for a time~ knowing they have but passed beyond
the horizon of mortal eyes into immortality.

Devotional Prayer:
Almighty and Eternal God! We pause now in reme~brance of all our
departed Brethren. We realize with awe and wonder that birth and de.ath are
natural parts of human life. We thank Thee for thy love does contmue to
surround us. May the dedication and love of all our Brethren "".ho hav~ gone
before us inspire us to exalted and exemplary character, to unfe1gne? piety to
God, and to fidelity of our trust. 0 God, grant us a . new c.ommJtment to
Freemasonry. At this very m~ment m~y we vow, once agam, to follow the tenets
and teachin~s of our Fraternity that, m due season, we may be called to that all
perfect, glorious, and celestial Lodge above, where the Supreme Grand Master
of the Universe forever presides. Amen.

TAXES
All Bureaus filed the required information with the Internal Revenue
Service and with the State Franchise Tax Board. Bureaus required to file tax
returns did so and filed them on time.

BUSH MASONIC RELIEF FUND
The. Bush Masonic Relief provides operating funds for the five Bureaus
located 10 the greater Los Angeles area. The contributions from this fund
amounted ~o more than 66% of the total income for the seventeen Bureaus and
we appreciate this generous contribution for operations in the greater Los
Angeles area.
Several of our Bureaus operate blood ban.ks for the benefit of California
Masons and ~heir families as well as for sojourners. One thousand two hundred
forty-five units of blood were donated during the year and 556 units were
released to provide this important life support to our members, their families

OPERATING EXPENSES
Total cost for operating the seventeen Bureaus for the year ending June 30,
1989 amounted to $168,891.81. Fixed expenses were $107,179.89; telephone,
printing and postage were $17,433.09 and taxes were $9,204.22. Some Executive
Secretaries receive a modest salary while others receive no salary. A few choose
to receive mileage only.

CONCLUSIONS
Special appreci~tion and thanks are expressed to the Grand Master, Most.
Worshipful Stanley L. Channon, and his Grand Lod~e office staff for their
continued support and to the Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful Sam M.
Pavlovich, for his assistance as our liaison officer. We also thank the Grand
Secretary, Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, who spoke to us at our Oakland
meeting and who provided continuing help throughout the year.
Appreciation is also expressed to the Presidents, officers and representatives of all Bureaus in this Grand Jurisdiction for therr great and continued
interest in and devotion to the activities of the various Bureaus and for their
help to our sojourning Brethren and their families.
Our Executive Secretaries deserve special note as they are in the forefront
of our fraternal and charitable business and are on call every day and night of
the year. These men are the backbone of our Bureaus and to each we express
our deep and abiding appreciation for their work.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT

GRAND MASTER'S ACHIEVEMENT AWARDS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Our sixteen member Committee meets quarterly during the year. One of
our Committee meetings takes place at Grand Lodge, such to encourage Grand
Lodge attendance. Our areas of interest and responsibility include:
Grand Master's Achievement Award Program: This year we approved 165
applicants. To paraphrase one of our District Inspectors, ''This program is one
of the best in California. It provides me with the leverage I need to keep everyone
working to meet a minimum standard.". Our Commiltce is pleased with this
program as it encourages and provides assistance for a Lodge to plan and
budget alon~ with a multitude of other assistance. It is interesting, in reviewing
the applications, to see the annual Lodge activities. This, along with the points
earned, is a good indicator of how a Lod~e is doing. This year we had twe~ve
new first year recipients and thirty-three sixth year recipients. This outstanding
program can help keep self imposed pressure on each succeeding Master to
keep his year as interesting and successful as those before him. Inspectors also
use the program for similar reasons.
Lodge Leadership Handbook: Last year our Grand Lodge Booth and the
Book Store sold over 200 of these fine handbooks. This handbook provides the
"how to", forms and form letters to enable the Senior Lodge officers to plan,
budget and execute a successful year ac; Master.
Lodge Presentations: Our Committee members are available to meet with
Lodges in trouble, discuss problem areas, make recommendations for improvement and most important, be there to help. Generally problem areas involve
Officer Development, Lodge Attendance, Lodge ActiVIties and Membership
Development. This service is available to Lodges and they are encouraged to
take advantage of it as needed. Request cards are available in our Grand Lodge
Booth and we also hand them out in the Leadership Handbook.
New opportunities include our assisting with the membership problem. '.f he
answers from 800 questionnaires received last year provide us with an insight
we are currently working on to pass on to Grand Lodge. We have a ~oal t_o
submit some programs and possibly resolutions next year to assist with this
endeavor.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

33

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting to the
Brethren of the Grand Lodge on the financial condition of the Grand Lodge
and its entities which include the Masonic Homes of California, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple and the California Masonic Foundation.
An examination of the several financial statements as of June 30, 1989, was
made by Lindquist, von Husen and Joyce, Certified Public Accountants, San
Francisco. Their complete reports are an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's
Report. Since you as members of the Grand Lodge are, in effect, the stockholders of these institutions, your reading and study of the fmanci.al statements
is encouraged.

In these times of fiscal deficits by some factions of government, it is
noteworthy that all of the organizations of Grand Lodge have operated within
their income and the confines of their budgets. All assets and investments are
well managed and secure.
On the other hand, the current decline in membership and escalating costs
are admonitions that future financial planning be prudent and conservative.
Masonic activities in California should not be curtailed because of a lessening
in membership. At the same time, every effort should be made to assure that
funds are only spent on that which will bring the greatest return and benefit to
the Freemasons of this State.
We are grateful for the continued generosity of the members of this great
Fraternity, for the coope.ration and support of Grand Master Stanley L. Channon and his officers, for that of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes,
California Masonic Memorial Temple and the California Masonic Foundation
and especially for the dedication of the accounting staff of Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
Ralph H. Head, Grand Treasurer

Referred to the Committee on Distribution. That Committee referred the
entire report of the Grand Treasurer to the Committee on Finance. (The Grand
Treasurer's Report also included copies of the audits of the several Masonic
Entities.)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Consolidation of Lodges (C.M.C. 2104)

All requirements of the law with respect to consolidations of Lodges having
been complied with, authorization is requested to properly endorse the
Charters of the following Lodges:
Norwalk Lodge No. 315 and Centennial Lodge No. 729, effective October
1, 1988 to be known as Norwalk Lodge No. 315.

'

Most Worshipful Grand Master, distinguished guests and Brethren. The
negative part of our report will inform you that the past year has brought the
greatest number of consolidations of Masonic Lodges in California Masonic
History. Through September 30, 1989, Grand Master Channon has approved
the consolidation of twenty-nine Lodges and additional consolidations are in

36

PROCEEDING S OF THE

progress. The positive part of our report will inform you of the progress of
Lodges which have been granted dispensations or charters since our last Grand
Lodge session.
Three Stars Lodge No. 839 in San Diego was chartered on November 11,
1988. Since that time it has received petitions for and conferred twenty-three
first degrees, sixteen second degrees and twelve third dewees. Six new members
have been received by affiliation. It is qualified to receive the Grand Master's
Achievement Award. Its prospects for the future are equally bright.
Sunrise Lodge No. 840 in Reseda was chartered on November 12, 1988.
Since that time it has conferred several first and second degrees, three third
degrees and received several new members by affiliation. Worshipful Master
Joe Winchell reports that the Lodge is active and doing well and that the officers
and members are weU pleased with its progress.
Fox-Coates Daylight Lodge U.D. in Victorville was instituted on August
22, 1989. It is located in a rapidly expanding high desert recreational and
retirement area There are many California Masons and sojourners in the area.
Many are reluctant or unable to travel considerable distances at night. The
daylight Lodge provides an opportunity for Masonic participation that l?reviously was not available to them. The Lodge is continuing the active participation in Masonic and community activities that were initiated by the predecessor
Masonic Club. In consideration of the short time that the Lodge has been in
operation it bas requested that its dispensation be extended through September
30, 1990. It is the recommendatio n of your Charters Committee that its request
be granted.
Irvine Lodge U .D . in Irvine was instituted on April 23, 1989. It is located
in one of the most rapidly e"l>anding areas of Southern California which
previously did not have a Masoruc Lodge in the immediate area. At the time of
dispensation, a meeting place in Irvine was not available. It now has a permanent
meeting place in Irvine and on September 23rd, conferred its first third degree .
It now has three petitions for the degrees and several petitions for affiliation.
The Lodge bas requested that it be granted a charter. It is the recommendatio n
of the Charters Committee that its request be granted.
That portion of the Grand Secretary's Report dealing with change of

meetin~ place of Lodges under Sections 2098 and 2100 of the California

Masomc Code and the consolidation of Lodges under Section 2104 of the
California Masonic Code has been referred to this Committee for consideration. We find that all of the requirements of our laws have been complied with
and recommend that the Grand Secretary be authorized to properly endorse
the charters of those Lodges. A listing of those Lodges is included as a part of
the Grand Secretary's Report.

After the conviction and sentence, which was affirmed on appeal, charges
of Unmasonic conduct were filed on October 21, 1981. He was found "Guilcy"
of U nmasonic conduct and the penalty was fixed at Expulsion. This was affirmed
by Grand Lodge in October, 1982.
He applied for restoration in 19?7 and tha~ petition was denied by GraJ!d
Lodge in October, 1988. He now agam seeks remstatemen l and has on.cc agru_n
submitted several letters of personal reference and recommenda llon. HIS
Lodge has not responded to notice of his petition although timely advised.
Your Committee feels that due to the severe natwe of the violation and the
lack of evidence of remorse or rehabilitation by the petitioner, we recommend
that his petition again be denied.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2278
In Trial Record No. 2278 a member of Temescal Lodge No. 314 was
charged with three specifications of unmasonic conduct alleging willfully failing
lo file income tax returns with the intent to evade payment during the years 1981
through 1983.
Your Committee on Trial Review reviewed this matter during Grand
Lodge in 1988 and recommende d that the matter be returned lo Temescal
Lodge because of procedural error although the Trial Master had found the
member guilty. Grand Lodge adopted your Committee's recommenda tion and
returned the matter for a new trial in accordance with our opinion.
In April 1989 the member received a Masonic Trial and was found not
guilty. Your Trial Review Committee, after extensive review of the trial record
respectfully disagrees with the Commission's findings. The evidence contained
in the record clearly indicates that the member is guilty of unmasonic conduct.
This evidence includes:

1. The member admitted that he did not file tax returns for three years.
2. The member was found guilty of failing to file a tax retwn after
pleading Nolo \ontendere in Superior Court.
California Masonic Code Section 3302 provides that "Any violation of the
criminal laws of the United States or of any other governmenta l entity by a
Mason involving moral turpitude shall constitute unmasonic conduct sufficient
to support the filing of charges against such Mason."
Willful failure to file tax returns for the purpose of evading the payment of
income taxes is an offense involving moral tlll1>itude. Therefore, based on all
the evidence in the record and the relevant proVlsions of the California Masonic
Code, the member is guilty of unmasonic conduct
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED , that the fmdingofthe Commission be reversed, a fmding
of guilty be entered, and the penalty be fixed at suspension.
Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2299
In Trial Record No. 2299, a member of Clovis Lodge No. 417 was charged
with two (2) specifications of unmasonic conduct.
Trial by Commission resulted in a finding of not guilty on all specifications
and a fmding of not guilty of unmasonic conduct. The Commissioners then made
a finding that the accused should be reprimanded in open Lodge.
Your Committee on Trial Review found that the Trial Record as submitted
to Grand Lodge was sufficient to support the findings of not guilty of all
specifications and a finding of not guilty of urunasonic conduct. However, your
Committee believes that there can be no reprimand in open Lodge where there
has been a finding of npt guilty as to all specifications and a finding of not guilty
as to unmasonic conduct.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2299 the findings of not guilty
of all specifications and the finding of not guilty of unmasonic conduct
be affirmed but that the finding of reprimand in open Lodge be
stricken.
Report ADOPTED.
Respectfully submitted,

Report ADOPTED.

REPORTOFTHEGRANDLECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Brethren, at the outset, I take this opportunity to express my "Thank You"
for the great privilege of serving this Grand Lodge as its Grand Lecturer.
Our statutes state that it is the duty of the Grand Leeturer to present a
report relating to ritual at each Annual Communication. Acrordingly, I report
as follows:
All of the ritu.al, to its minutest detail, has been reviewed throughout the
entire Jurisdiction. Conferences were held in each division where each depee,
lecture, and Candidate's proficiency was exemplified by the Inspectors m an
impressive manner. We are both fortunate to have and appreciative of the
services of these dedicated servants of the Craft.

As in the prior year, seminars were conducted at randomly selecte.d locations throughout the Jurisdiction. These seminars afforded the Grand Lecturer
the opportunity to meet with the Brethren on a one-on-one basis to review and
discuss ritual and to create a closer relationship with the Lodges. This program
continues to be well received and must be continued and expanded.
As we travelled extensively from one end of this Jurisdiction to the other,
conducting seminars and participating in and witnessing various ceremonies,
we were impressed with the enthusiasm and the tenacity of the man¥ "small"
Lodges struggling to maintain their identity in their respective commurutics and
we laud them for their efforts. Yet far too many Lodges found it necessary to
consolidate and many more are now tottering on the brink of extinction for lack
of interested or qualified Brethren who arc willing to serve as officers.

Everywhere we went we heard increasingly urgent cries for help in improving the performance of your ritualistic responsibilities. Much of the work we
saw was good, but much, much more needs to be done if we are to regain the
stature of ritual which this Jurisdiction once enjoyed. You have convinced us
that much more help than we have been able to give you is needed. As you are
aware, the Brethren assembled at the last Annual Communication adopted
legislation permitting the possession and use of a cipher ritual in this Jurisdiction. Two resolutions asking adoption of a specific cipher were submitted for
your consideration at this Annual Commumcation, and, while one has since
been withdrawn, it has become clear that sentiment throughout our Jurisdiction
is in favor of adoption. Tomorrow you are going to be voting on that resolution
which remains. Resolution 89-2 recognizes that that book which purports to be
California ritual contains many errors and asks adoption of only those parts
which conform to the ritual now taught and used in this J urisdicllon.
Next May I shall have been a Mason for half a century. I never dreamed
that I would be saying what I am about to say. Your wishes both as demonstrated
at the last Annual Communication and as expressed to us during this last year
leave us with little choice. IfJou adopt Resolution 89-2, your Committee on
Ritual pledges to prepare an publish corrections to that cipher. We d o so to
provide you with the best at our disposal. It is with great sadness and serious

PROCEEDlNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

misgivings that we take this action that we have argued against for so long. Not
only do we feel that we may be compromising our obligation, but ~e also _fear
that even a comple.te and correct cipher will not result in the quahly of ~tual
that our Candidates deserve and have a right to expect. At the same tune,
however we cannot compromise the ritual we have learned and taught, and
abandod it to some approximation merely for convenience.

Meetings of the Trustees are usually held on the first Wednesday of the

The meetings are frequently attended by the Chairman of the Endowment
Board, as well as some of the Endowment Board members.
Many Committee meetings are held on the Tuesday evening preceding the
regular meetings. Many of the Committee reports are pre£ared in advance for
distribution at or prior to the regular meeting. It is very difficult to cover all of
the items that need discussion, consideration and action in the amount of time
available.

UNION CITY FACILITIES
The maintenance of a facility the size of our Home, consists of a myriad of
problems of all kinds and description. They are constant and range from small
additions and changes, to problems in electrical, plumbing, telephone, water,
etc. in a never ending stream.
In addition, the staff completed the laundry remodel, investigated a potential bank and road slippage, completed another portion of the energy saving
program covering general lighting, installed a new switchboard at the reception
area, revised the phone and alarm system in the existing buildings and prepared
the existing systems for tie-in to the new additions.
A more serious problem arose because of environmental agency concerns
about an abandoned fuel tank. About ten years ago, the tank was found to be
leaking. It was abandoned and filled in accordance with and under the supervision of the Union City Fire Department.
Currently the emphasis is on environmental issues. The State of California
asked Union City to identify abandoned tanks which necessitated our being
required to remove the tank. Environmental geologists are being employed to
determine the extent of the contamination, if any, and removal and disposal of
the soil.
In addition, ground water monitoring wells will be required and if lower
level contamination is found, a water treatment prow.am will be put into effect.
The extent of the problem is not known at this wnting, but the cost could be
substantial.

by William W. Dickson, Chainnan, Physical Facilities Committee
UNION CITY EXPANSION
The current year saw the completion of the new Simino ff Center and Lorber
Skilled Nursing Facility. Formal dedication ceremonies were conducted by
Grand Master Channon and the Grand Lodge Officers on May 7, 1989.
In the Siminoff Center, which consists of a chapel and Lodge room, the
design attempted to convey a feeling of historical continuity. Bricks from the
old Siminoff T emple built m 1903 were used to face a wall of the new Lodge
room. The altar and furniture of the respective stations were reconditioned. The
combination gas/electric chandeliers and entry room hour glass used in 1903
were completely refurbished and provide a spectacular example of the
craftsmanship of a prior age carefully restored by a modern skilled silversmith.
The Lorber facility is in the process of being stocked with inventory and
readied for licensing inspections. Residents will be transferred from the Wollenberg Facility to Lorber about November 1st.
Plans are being made to then remodel the Wollenberg Facility. This facility
was built in 1960 and has had heavy use since. Due to changes in our population,
nursing concepts and licensing requirements, this will be a major remodel to
provide for current needs.

COVINA ADULT ,FACILITIES EXPANSION
A formal dedication ceremony was conducted by Grand Master Channon
and the Grand Lodge Officers on April 9, 1989. Shortly thereafter, due to
intergovernmental changes and a new Fire Officer for the local fire district, we
were required to fire sprinkler the existing administration building, offices,
kitchen, dining room, parlor and infrrmary. This in in process as of this writing
and is scheduled for completion by September 15th.
The contractor, Tilden-Coil Constructors, Inc. has been most cooperative
and has provided us with a picture setting.
COVINA FACILITY
This facility again required only a very nominal expenditure for routine
replacements of property and equipment. Coordinatin~ with the contractor for
shut down tic-ins of the new work to the old, protection of the children and
pe rsonae~ as well as familiarizaiton training with new mechanical, electrical,
frre and sound systems occupied a portion of staff time.
Regarding the telephone system, it should be noted that Brother Gary
Mason of Mizpah Lodge No. 378, assisted by a group of Masons from the
Telephone Club of Los Angeles, made a substantial contribution of time, talent
and resources to install all the telephone conduit and wiring for the entire new
facility at no expense to the Homes.

Our most unusual problem this year is the development of an underground
leak in the pond at Rainbow Park. The assumption at present is that it is caused
by tunneling of some ground squirrels. A squirrel abatement program is in force
and investigations are being made to d etermine the source of the leak, extent
of the undermining and solution of the problem.

For many years the Board of Trustees operated without the benefit of a
formal Admissions Committee. In o rder to maximize the operating efficiency
of the Board, a formal Committee within the Board of Trustees was implemented. This has allowed the Board to consider all applicants for admission
and provided sufficient time to carefully consider other important business
matters that are an essential part of a Corporation such as ows.

SCHOLARSHIPS
by Ronald A. Sherod, Chainnan, Scholarship Committee
For many years Masons and non-Masons alike have bestowed, through
Wills and other means, funds both specified and non-specified for the education
of ow youth at our Covina Masonic Home for Children. Your Board of
Trustees, over the years, and through very prudent and sound investments
policies, has protected every dollar of those Trusts and has been able to provide
the necessary scholarship funds to deserving students solely from the earnings
derived from those initial Trusts. Based on specific need, each applicant is
evaluated and, if approved, is awarded either a Grant, Loan or a combination
thereof to continue a formal education in an approved institution of their choice.
Scholarships are limited based on the selected academic level such as Junior
Colleges, Vocational Schools, State Colleges, Universities and Post Graduate
work. These award limits range from $4,000.00 to $6,900.00 per school year
based on the appropriate academic level. Each student receiving scholarship
funds is required to provide proof of earned ~ade point averages in order to
continue receiving this support. Your Masomc H omes of California Trustees
are proud to report to you the following actions for the 1989/1990 academic year
as well as key historical scholarship data.
During this past Masonic year your Board of Trustees approved the
continuation of scholarship support of four ( 4) former resident/graduates of our
Covina H ome. In addition, we approved two (2) first time applicants for
scholarship support. In all, six (6) applicants are currently receiving scholarship
support in the aggregate of $26,234.00 for this school year. This averages
$4,372.00 per student for this school year.
Over the past eleven (11) years a total of $298,693.00 has been awarded to
thirty-three {33) former and deserving residents. This averages $9,051.00 per
student to educate a former resident. Undoubtedly, this is one of the best
investments Masons have ever made!
ADMISSIONS REPORT
by Jack R. Vickers and Alvin J. Weis, Co-Chainnen, Admissions Committee
The Admissions Committee of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California consists of eight members of the twelve member Board.
The Committee has Co-Chairmen. Currently, Alvin J. Weis serves as C hairman
in the North and Jack R . Vickers as Chairman in the South. They are supported
by six other members of the Board of Trustees; three each from the Northern
and Southern part of the State. The evaluations of the full Committee on all
applicants for admission to our Masonic Homes is presented by the Chairmen
to the Board for their approval. The Board meets monthly, alternating in the
North at the Union City Home and in the South at the Children's Home in
Covina.

75

Several years ago, it became necessary to establish a waiting list due to an
increased number of applicants for admission to our Home for Adults. During
this period the Board adopted a point rating system to insure that each applicant
would be admitted to the Home based upon the applicant's need regardless of
when the application was approved. This system is constantly being evaluated
and revised by the Board in an endeavor to provide assistance to the most needy.
Our new Administrator at Union City has implemented a different mode of
operation which minimizes the necessity of a waiting list at the present time. A
point rating system has not been required at the Children's Home in Covina,
however, all applicants are given the same thoughtful and careful consideration
as those at Union City.
REAL ESTATE REPORT
by Hambleton F. Leas, Chairman, Real Estate Committee
The R eal Estate Committee of the Masonic Homes, composed of
Hambleton F. Leas, Sam M. Pavlovich and Gerald L. Sharer, continues to be
an active unit in the operation of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes.
Real Property is made available to the Masonic Homes of California by
direct grant, from admissions to the Home fo r life estates, from Wills and other
sowces.
During the past year, sales of r eal property have exceeded $1,000,000.00.
Oil and gas leases have been renewed and easements granted for the development of potential oil and gas fields.
As of September 1, 1989, we had an inventory of unsold properties consisting of a lot, eight (8) mobile homes, eight (8) single family residences and 515
acres of pasture land near Rio Vista, California.
When new Residents enter the home, their former residence is not sold for
ninety (90) days. After ninety days, a release is signed, stating that they have no
intention of withdrawing from the Masonic Home and they authorize the sale
of their former place of residence. This is o ne reason we always have an
inventory of unsold properties.

INSURANCE
by Sam M. Pavlovich, Chairman, Insurance Committee
Excalating premium costs for Homes employees' medical coverage have
necessitated a review and subsequent change in providers. Medical benefits for
our Northern California employees (Union City and San Francisco) are now
being provided through the Bay Pacific HMO plan. Our Covina employees are
covered by Inter-Valley, also an HMO provider. Substantial savings have
resulted in the change to the HMO plans. These were used to provide additional
benefits to all employees. The benefits consist of a pre-paid dental plan, a
pre-paid vision plan, and group life insurance in the amount of $10,000.00.
Optional benefits include supplemental dental and vision care as well as an
optional package consisting of medical, dental, and child care expenses which

POLICIES
by Roy J. Hen ville, Chainnan, Policy Committee
The ongoing operation of our Masonic Homes are guided by Policy
adopted by the Board of Trustees. As times and conditions change, so do our
policies need to be changed to insure a smooth and efficient operation to meet
current needs.
The present Policy Manual, for the most part, was written in 1983. There
have been additions and changes each year smce that time. Sometimes there
are detail changes that may be considered minor but do contribute to ease of
understanding.
Thls year there has been the usual pattern of Policy changes with one
notable change. The Board of Trustees has usually followed a practice of
requiring a majority vote on all Board action. That policy has been changed.
Relative to matters pertaining to Admission of Applicants or for non-resident
assistance, a majonty vote will still govern. On all other business matters a
three-fourths favorable vote will be required for adoption.

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
MASONIC HOME, COVINA
1988-1989
It is not only with pleasure but excitement that I offer this report to the
Grand Lodge.
O~ care program at Covina is abou~ to expand. We are soon going to serve

both children and the elderly. Construction of 56 aP.artments and a community
~ce building is substantially complete. On April 9, 1989, the Grand Lodge

laid.the cornerstone and dedicated this expansion project. Over 2,000 Masons,

family and friends witnessed this historic event. Final construction refinements

and operating program procedures are now being completed before we com-

~en~ this new operation. Soon the wisdom of the elderly., the strength and

Yllality of childre n, and the beauty of them both will adorn this Masonic Home.

pur Masonic Home has raised nearly 1,800 children since 1899. We have
IUMved and served during two World Wars, the great depression, epidemics
and an era of domestic stress.

This year we have served 39 children. Four children have reached maturity
and have graduated. Two were reunited with their families. Our Jurisdiction is
one of only nine in America which continue to serve children. Our population
is at its lowest point in. our history.
Prudence says we must carefully examine why this is so. It is difficult to
imagine that our mission is completed. This child care program is dedicated to
the relief of qualified Masons and their wives or widows. We have over 150,000
members in this Jurisdiction and as many wives or widows. We have a capacity
for 80 children in our Home. Given our present vacancy, if only 2/lOO's of 1%
of those whom we are delegated to serve needed relief, our Home would be
efficiently used.

If our mission is not complete, then perhaps we, as Masons, are not aware
of who can be served in this Home. The yardstick is Masonic relief. Children,
grandchildren, nieces, nephews, or step-children of qualified Masons, who are
related by blood or marriage, may be admitted to this Home.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple hereby
submits its 34th Annual Report.
At the close of the 1988 Annual Communication of the Grand Lod~e, the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its organizational meeting as required by the California Masonic Code, nominating
and electing the following officers for the ensuing year:
Robert A Bush
Robert 0. West
Ralph H. Head
Robert A. Klinger

President
Vice President
Treasurer
Secretary

The California Masonic Memorial Temple is a public and patriotic monument dedicated to the members of the armed services and the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of California, and its constituent Lodges, who gave their lives in
battle during World War II that the citizens of the United States might continue
to enjoy their freedom and the ability to live, act, speak and think without
restraint.
FINANCIAL RESERVES
In 1988 the Articles of Incofl>Oration were amended to provide for establishing financial reserves for repalTS, upkeep and maintenance. These reserves
are in the process of being created.
To assist the Board in determining the life expectency of major equipment,
professional assistance was sought. When the Industrial Inspection was completed, the report indicated all major equipment appears to be in excellent
condition. This is due to an excellent preventative maintenance program by the
Memorial Temple engineers; bearing in mind, the normal life expectency of
major equipment is between 20 and 30 years.
EARTHQUAKE INSURANCE
On the recommendation of the Grand Lodge Insurance Committee, the
Memorial Temple purchased Earthquake Insurance in a package policy with
the Masonic Homes of California. Coverage is for 30 million dollars for any one
earthquake, encompassing individually or collectively, the Memorial Temple,
the four (4) Pine Street parcels (behind the Temple), and the Masonic Homes
of California at Union City and Covina. The coverage is all inclusive with a five
percent (5%) deductible for property, furniture, equipment, updated building
code standards in the event o total loss (to a total of 5 million d ollars), and lost
income. The Memorial Temple premium share is $56,500.00.
UNRESTRICTIVE GRANT
The Geor$e H. Sandy Foundation gave an unrestrictive grant of $4,000.00
to the Memonal Temple in recognition and encouragement to the Memorial
Temple to continue the valuable services that are presently rendered to the
community.

GRANDLODGEOFCALWORNIA

103

MEMORIAL TEMPLE GARAGE
The Memorial Temple Garage is presently in the sixth year of a ten year
lease without any options for extension or sub-leasing. Income approaches a
gross of $500,000.00 to the Leasee with $300,000.00 to the Memonal Temple.
Your Board has been concerned with the increased operating expenses
confronting Grand Lodge which is reflected in the annual rate of the per capita
tax to each subordinate Lodge. Considerable time has been spent this year
discussing and conducting a feasibility study to determine whether the Grand
Lodge of California, should or should not, lease, operate and maintain the
Memorial Temple Garage when the pre-sent lease expires on April l, 1993.
Professional assistance was again solicited to research this feasibility question. In the opinion of our auditing f1Tm which conducted this study, the report
concluded their would be no tax problem, consequence or conflict with the
Internal Revenue Service to either the Grand Lodge of California or to the
California Memorial Temple. However, the report did indicate the increased
income would be considered as "unrelated income" and would produce a tax
consequence equivalent to a corporate tax of 34% .
This has been brought lo the attention of the Executive Committee for their
consideration and recommendation.
It is the opinion of the Memorial Temple Board of Trustees that a decision
should be reached not later than the Annual Communication of October 1991
to effective~y coordinate, plan and organize the operation and managem~nt of
the Memonal Temple Garage when the present lease expires.
GRAND WOGE LIJJRARY AND MUSEUM
The Grand Lodge Library and Muse um is funded by the Memorial T emple
and has an approved bu~get for 1989-1990 of $28,200.00. The Library is open
for your pleasure and en1oyment Monday through Friday (except for holidays)
by the staff of the Library and the C hairman of the Comm1ttee, C. John Bellman,
Jr.
ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
Your Board of Trustees wishes to acknowledge the continuous assistance,
cooperation and dedication provided by the Executive Vice President and

Varnum Pa~; the Grand Treasurer; the Grand Secretary; and to the Manager
of Accountmg, Hugo Delfin, for each of their valuable contributions to the
Trustees this past year.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:

The California Masonic Foundation was established in 1969 by the Grand
Lodge as a non-profit cb.aritable corporation under the laws of tbe State of
California, for the furtherance of all phases of education, charitable and scientific purposes. The Foundation was tnitially funded by the proceeds from the
sale of the Masonic Club houses adjacent to the campus of the University of
California at Berkeley and Los Angeles. In 1972, the Order of the Amaranth
conveyed a trust fund to the Foundation in token of their support of the
Foundation's scholarship program. Two additional adjunct funds have been
established through the generous contributions of Mrs. Robinson and Brother
Harry Walker Lister. These contributions enhanced by the support of the
Lodges and members of this Grand Lodge have created a net worth in excess
of $1.6 million dollars. (Contributions to the General fund exceeded $38,000.00
this year.) The interest accruing this year from these funds, has provided
$7,500.00 to aid our Masonic youth groups with their leadership tratning and
$109,750.00 has been distributed to 143 deserving students in the form of
unrestricted scholarships.
While the scholarship program has been the single thrust of the Foundation
since its creation, the Foundation has now matured to tbe point where it can
expand its influence and perform a major educational and charitable service to
society. Beginning last year, the Foundation undertook the support of the Grand
Lodge's "Drug and Alcohol Abuse Educational Program". President Bush's
initiative on the "War Against Drugs" clearly needs the help, aid and assistance
of all concerned citizens - we must all do all we can to conquer this extreme
threat to our nation. The Foundation clearly sees this as a great opportunity to
solicit the help of the friends of our Fraternity to join with us to provide
assistance to the drug and alcohol abuse educational programs in the schools
in our State. This program is operated through the school superintendents and
provides Masonry with tbe vehicle to directly participate in this battle. You
cannot pick up a newspaper without seeing several articles which define the
magnitude of the Drug and Alcohol Abuse problem throughout the United
States. The menace of illegal drugs requires all concerned citizens to join
together to provide an integrated multi-fronted attack. The time has come for
us to do everything possible to ensure that the entire population will just "SAY
NO TO DRUGS".
While much is published about the fight against illegal drugs, it should be
pointed out the abuse oflegal drugs also presents a si~ificant danger. One out
.o f eight prescriptions wr~tten ~ th~ United States is for a d~ug t~a~ affects
moods, thoughts or behavior. Likewise, the number of drunk dnvers is mcreasing at an alarming rate, especially amon$ women drivers. In North Carolina, the
number of women arrested for OWi's mcreased by 43% last year. According
to MADD, drunk driving kills more than 23,000 Umted States people each year
and injures an additional 560,000.
!~e ducatio~al prograi;n sponsor~d ~y l~e Grand Lodge is directed at
proVIding educational matenals for the JUIDOr high and elementary level student
to aid the professional teaching staff with their efforts to bring the message of

This has been a difficult year for the Foundation, but the Trustees are

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Your Committee on Credentials is pleased to submit this report of the 140th
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge.

HA~AII: The special and long standing relationship between the Masons
of Hawau ~nd Califo rnia took o n new meaning and significance this year with
the formation of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Hawaii.
The strong affection between the Brethren of both Jurisdictio ns dates back at
l~ast to May 5, 1882, when H~waii became part of the Grand Lodge of Califorrua, and will under the benign eye of the Great Architect of the Universe
~ntinue undiminished into the future. After diligent investigation, the Committee on June 6, 1989 recommended to Grand Master Stanley L. Channon that
the .Gr~d Lodge of Ha~a!i be officially recognized by the Grand Lodge of
C:aliforrua as a regular, legitimate and official Masonic Grand Lodge due all the
nghts and benefits of such recognition.

Again we wish to express our thanks to the Grand Secretary and his office
staff for their help.

Grand Master Channon made such recognition and installed the new corps
of Hawaiian Grand Lodge Officers on July 1, 1989.

ITALY: Since the early 1970's, the Commission on Information for Recognition, along with other jurisdictional Committees including this one, hav~ b~en
concerned with the quality of Freemasonry in Italy. In 1986, th~ n~w consht~lt~n
adopted by the Grand Orient of Italy, was deemed to have eliminated behef m
God and the volume of the sacred law as essential parts of the furniture of the
Lodge, thus eliminating the third standard of recognition. Consequently, recognition of the Grand Orient was withheld.
Since that time, ongoing and exhaustive evaluation and. investig<1:tion, including meetings and correspondence has a~ded new mforma~1on <if:ld
knowledge. It is believed now that the Gr.and Onent of. I~aly has reviewe~ its
past and re-evaluated its future as to what is expected of 1t 10 fraternal relah~n­
ship with North American Masonic bodies, particularly in respect to the belief
in the Supreme Being and the volume of the sacred law.
Consequent to this contin~g re".11e, and j~ining in the ~animous. opinion
of the Commission on Informat1on, this CoD110.1ttee concurs m the findmgs that
the Grand Orient of Italy currently meets the standards of the Commissioi:;i for
recognition, and so recommends its recognition by the Grand Lodge of California.

Grand Assembly of this Confederation of 56 Grand Lodges of Central and
South America, Mexico and the Caribbean held last _Year. The A~se~bly
approved an ambitious plan to help undeveloped countries overcome c~1ttca1

REPORT OF THE COMMI TIEE
ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:
Freemason ry's membersh ip decline continues. In this year alone, the Grand
Lodge F .& A.M. of California lost 6,000 members, not counting the Masons in
Hawaii (who now have their own Grand Lodge). We lose Candidate s and we
lose members, both primarily because they don't understand Freemason ry.
Because they do not know enough about it, they cannot answer questions, and
they do not even wish to talk the subject, for they haven't the informatio n, and
they're unsure what they can say. Thus others, receiving either evasive answers,
or "I can't answer that", have the impression that ours is a "secret society" and
sus~ct that what we "hide" must be something bad. This we must change by
providing that informatio n to the Candidate s and members. We must, WE
MUST, educate them. In order to attract, and hold, that "good" man in the
community , we must each be a strong, outspoken proponent of Freemason ry.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON YOUTH ORDERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
With the unveiling of Most Worshipful Cbannon's theme, "Accent on
Youth" in 1988, this Committee's direction for the eosuin~ Masonic year became
immediately evident--to place the emphasis--(or accent)--on our own Masonic
Youth Groups. To more effectively carry out this the me, we increased the
Committee's size by 15 me mbe rs for a total of 49 hard working Brothers.
The year's work started by requesting all 1989 Worshipful Masters lo
appoint a "Lodge Youth Coordinator", and by virtue of Most W orshipful
Channon's letter to all the Lodges, 180 responses were received. We believe this
to be an important first step, laying the foundation for our next goal, which was
to open up or increase the lines o f communication b etween subordinate Lodges
and Youth Groups in their areas.
Committee members played a vital role in achieving the latter goal by
committing themselves to increased visitation to both their assigned Lodges and
the Assemblies, Bethels and C hapters in their assigned territories, and by
distributing 10,000 of the Grand Master's "official" pins wherever they went.
Passing out pins, while a seemingly insignificant act by itself, proved to be an
overwhelming success in opening doors, breaking the ice, and leaving our yo ung
peo~le and their adult leaders in approximately 150 Rainbow Assemblies, T37
Job s Daughter Bethels and 125 DeMolay Chapters with a most favorable
impression of M asons in California.
Many membe rs of this Committee are to be commended for their extra
effort and particula r expertise applied toward special projects undertaken this
year. Work began in January to revise the Committee's Scholarship Books.
Committeemen collected, updated and edited available scholarship information in their ho me computers and prepared it for direct trartsmission to the
printer. Two thousand finished books were ready for distribution by the annual
MA YO (Masonic Youth Orders Adult Leaders) meeting this past summer.
These have been shipped to the various State Adult Leaders and will be o r have
been distributed to every Assembly, Bethel and Chapter in California.
Committeemen in the Los Angeles area put in numerous hours, extra miles
on their cars, and made and received hundreds of phone calls in coordinating
all the details required to get our Public Service Announcement film for the
Youth Orders off the ground. Filming was completed on the 17th of Se ptember,
followed by editing. The finis hed product will be presented to ¥OU Brethren
during this program. It is our hope to get this 60 second film mto as many
television stations as possible in order to get our Youth Groups the publicity
and name recognition they so badly need and richly deserve.
At this time the Committe on Youth Orders wishes to express its profound
gratitude and appreciation to Sergei Goncharoff, Chairman, and his members
of the Film and Creative Projects Committee for their time, effort, patience,

118

PROCEE DINGS OF THE

professionalism and devotion to this project. Brethren , it would never have
happene d without you or the untold spent hours of Brothers AJton Emerson
and Donald Griffiths of this Committee.
At long last this Committee has implemented its Senior DeMolay Notification program wherein every DeMolay in California upon reaching his 21st
birthday, now receives a personal letter of congratulations from the Grand
Master. Each one of these letters is personalized and signed by the Grand
Master, thereby eliminating the "form letter" appearan ce. This year, over 1,000
such letters were mailed.
A Committee function continue d from prior years was the "Youth Extravaganza". This year's event was held in May in Arcadia. Once again, area
Committ eemen rallied to the call and pitched in to make the event a success for
the over 250 young people and adults in attendanc e.
Meetings were held for members of this Committee in both the Southern
and Northern parts of the State. Additionally, this Committee participa ted in
virtually all of the Leadersh ip Workshops by having an information table and
providing a youth speaker-- once again putting the local Lodges in direct contact
with our young people and bringing the needs of these groups to the attention
of the Brethren in California.
As in past years, this Committee has prepared an information package for
all Senior Wardens and we urge the Brethren to visit our booth on "G" floor and
pick up your packets. Our Committ ee members, staffing the booth, are most
anxious to answer your questions and are willing to assist you in any way possible
as you plan your Lodge programs for 1990--programs which will continue to put
the accent on youth.
This Committee's objectives still appear to be two-fold. To develop effective Fraterna l relations with the members and adult leaders of DeMolay ,
Rainbow and Job's Daughters, and to promote youth programs in the Lodges
and encourage the Lodge members to provide additional adult leadershi p to
their local youth groups. This latter goal continues to be a perplexing problem
which must be reached. Twenty years ago, our Masonic Youth Orders boasted
membership in all three orders of over thirty thousand members. Today these
same three organizations have less than 10,000. When any adult leader is asked
for his opinions as to the decline, the response is overwhelmingly the same. They
can get the new members but they can't keep them because of the lack of adult
support. Conversely, the Brethren report that the~ lose interest because of ~e
smaller numbers of Youth Members. These two altitudes are a "Catch 22" which
continues to promote the decline.
This Committee will continue to address this problem in 1990 through
increased visitation and presentations to both Lodges and Youth Orders.
Brethren, we must stem this tide. As these young people reach their majority,
we cannot expect them to show an active interest in joming our adult organizations, if we as adults, showed them little interest while they were maturing and
forming their opinions.
Your Committee on Youth Orders is pleased to report that it represen ted
the Grand Lodge at the following events througho ut the year:

how to approach the Committee with any business they wanted to have approved. It lS now very dated as a result of the more recent Grand Lodge changes

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
My Brethren of the Grand Lodge, I stand before you with mixed emotions.
The experience of the past four years, and more parttcularly the past year, has
been one of the most rewarding and enjoyable experiences of my life, thanks to
the cooperation and courtesies extended to me and the Grand Lodge officers
during the many visits to Lodges and Appendant and Concordant organizations.
On the other hand1 it has been somewhat disappointing to see Lodges consolidating and to witness the continual decline m membership and interest in
the Fraternity. As many of my predecessors have found, it is not easy to find
solutions to the problems which confront the Fraternity and to implement plans
for the correction of these problems.
THEME AND GOALS
It has been my firm conviction that the key to the future of the Fraternity is
YOUTH. I believe it is necessary to attract and involve younger members and
provide increased attention to the Masonic youth groups from which future
members maybe derived. The theme "ACCENT ON YOUTH" was chosen for
this year with those purposes in mind. Buttons were produced which contained
the square and compass and the theme in gold lettering on a blue background.
Thirty thousand of these pins were distributed to Masons throughout this
Jurisdiction and other Jurisdictions with enthusiastic reception. The same
theme pin with a kangaroo replacing the square and compass was distributed
to 15,000 non-Masons, spouses and youth groups as a further means of promoting the emphasis on youth. Banners showing these two pin designs were also
displayed at receptions throughout the Jurisdiction. Many compliments were
received from Masons and members of Appendant and Concordant organizations on the selection of this theme.
As a method of attracting younger men to the Fraternity, I chalJenged all
Masons in this Jurisdiction to seek out at least one young man in the age group
21-45 and endeavor to interest him in Freemasonry by inviting him to Masoruc
social functions, providing him with Masonic literature and being prepared to
answer questions about the Fraternity, i.e. information without solicitation.
Throughout the year, many younger men expressed concern about the Fraternity and a keen desire to follow-up on the theme.

STATE OF THE CRAFT
In spite of many problems throughout the Jurisdiction, Freemasonry in
Califorma is still generally strong but with numerous weak segments. Some
Lodges are flourishing; they have well planned activities and good attendance,
while others are struggling to stay in existence.
Aging of the membership continues to be a serious problem in many
respects. With an average age of more than 65, at least half of the members are
retired and are living on limited incomes. They are therefore reluctant to
approve large expenditures for Lodge activities. They are also the sideliners
who attend the Stated Meetings and vote on matters brought before the Lodge.
Because their interests are somewhat confined to their own experiences, there
is little opportunity for the Lodge to try new ventures.
Despite my challenge to all Masons to try and interest at least one young
man in the Fraternity, our net membership loss was larger than in the previous
year, even without the loss of the Hawaiian Brethren. This points up the urgency
of the membership problem quite dramatically. While numbers alone should
not be the criteria for evaluation of success, it is important to realize that the
services provided by the Grand Lodge which we are privileged to receive in
California have been made possible by the large membership and the associated
per capita. As the membership continues to decrease, the rer capita assessment
must necessarily increase to maintain the same level o service. Even more
important is the need to spend some funds for the purpose of attracting new
members by providing information and programs of interest. As a frame of
reference, the present per capita is approximately the cost of a modest meal, a
very small price to pay for the services provided.
The dearth of younger applicants not only keeps the average age high but
also reduces the number of available and eligible Brethren who can progress
thro ugh the chairs to become Master of the Lodge. In addition, the demands of
modern society diminish the time available for younger men to prepare themselves for their journey through the chairs. The result is that Lodges are having
increased difficulty in filling the stations. For similar reasons, the quality of the
Ritual is also suffering because of the lack of commitment on the part of many
officers.
Durin~ this year, there have been many consolidations of two or even three
Lod~es, pnmarily due to a Jack of officers, but also due to a lack of membership

participation. In some instances, financial considerations forced the consolidation.

GRAND LODGE OF HAWAII
After many previous attempts to form a Grand Lodge in the State of Hawaii,
the Brethren of the twelve (12) Hawaiian Lodges made their decision in the
early part of 1989 when nine (9) of the twelve (12) Lodges and 66 percent of the
voting Brethren voted in favor of such action. At its formation meeting on May
20, 1989, the principal officers were elected and By-Laws were adopted. Most
Worshipful William K. McKee, Jr., a native Hawaiian, was elected as the first
Grand Master. It was my pleasure to officially recognize the Grand Lodge of
Hawaii on June 9, 1989 after receiving assurance from the Chairman of the
Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges that the Hawaiian
Brethren had met the requirements for recognition. I was honored and
privileged to serve as the Installing Officer at the first Installation of Officers
on July 1, 1989. We offer our congratulations and extend the best wishes of lhe
Grand Lodge of California to the Grand Lodge of Hawaii in their new endeavor.

DECISIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Decision No. 1-/nterpretation of C.M.C. Section 2692
At the 1988 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, Carry-over Resolution No. 87-32 was adopted which amended Section 2086, Article IX, Section 1
of the California Masonic Code to provide that henceforth annual dues shall be
payable in advance on the first day of January, rather than quarterly on the first
days of January, April, July and October.

It has come to my attention that, by adopting this Resolution, a conflict has
been created with California Masonic Code Section 2692 concerning the payment of dues as a prerequisite to becoming a plural member or to obtaining a
Dimit for affiliation when transferring membership from one Lodge to another.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

147

Although Section 2692 provides in its sub-paragraphs 1st and 4th that a
member in this Jurisdiction must demonstrate that liis dues are paid through
"the next succeeding calendar quarter", the 1988 amendment from quarterly to
annual payment must supercede and make inapplicable the language relating
to quarterly payment.
It is therefore my Decision that Section 2692 of the California Masonic
Code be interpreted so that a member of this Jurisdiction seeking affiliation
either as a transferee or as a plural member must show that his dues are paid in
advance to December 31st of the year in which he seeks his Dimit or applies for
plural membership. If the transfer of membership from one Lodge to another
or the affiliation as a plural member cannot be accomplished and completed
prior to December 31st, the member must show that his dues are paid through
December 31st of the following year.
To carry out the intent of this Decision, I recommend that the words,
"through at least the ne:xt succeeding calendar quarter" be deleted from the first
r.aragraph of California Masonic Code Section 2692-1st and the words,
throug}:i the next succeeding calendar quarter" be deleted from California
Masonic Code Section 2692-4th.
It is further my Decision that upon issuance of a Dimit or Discontinuance
of Multiple Membership, a Lodge shall pro-rate a member's dues as of the end
of the calendar month in which the Dimit or Discontinuance is issued and refund
any excess dues which have been paid in advance.
I further recommend that Annotation 20861 be amended by changing the
words "effective at the end of the current quarter" to "effective at the end of the
current year".
I further recommend that Annotation 2086m be amended by changing the
words "in advance of the current quarter" to "in advance of the current month".
I further recommend that Annotations g and b to California Masonic Code
Section 2692 and Annotations 2800a and 2.814a be repealed.
Decision No. 2--Naming a Lodge Room in Honor of a Brother Mason
A Lodge in this Jurisdiction wished to name a Lodge room in a new Te mple
building in honor of a living member of the Lodge. The question was raised as
to whether this action would be in violation of Section 2002 of the California
Masonic Code which states, "No dispensation shall be granted for a new Lodge
\\ith a name similar to an existing Lodge, nor shall any name selected have for
its purpose the memorializing of a living person".

This Section addresses the naming of a Lodge and does not refer to a
building or a room within a building. No other Section of the California Masonic
Code is applicable to the question.
It is therefore my Decision that it is proper to name a Lodge room within
a Masonic Temple in honor of a Brother Mason, whether living or deceased.

Recommendation No. 1-Termination of Committees
By-Laws and Travel Allowances
Section 1202 of the California Masonic Code includes the Committees on
By-Laws and Travel Allowances as Standing Committees of the Grand Lodge.
Any change in a Standing Committee requires the approval of the Grand Lodge.
The decline in membership and the absence of new Lodges being formed
have .resulted in a decline in the need for a Committee to review By-Laws.
Routme amendments to the By-Laws of Lodges are handled administratively
by the Grand Secretary's office. Dispensations are handled by application to
and approval by the Grand Master.
The By-Laws Committee Chairman has also questioned the need for
continuation of this Committee on the basis that its activities are primarily
limited to auditing the actions taken during the year by the Grand Secretary.

by the Grand Secrelarys office in any case, and checks which are not picked up
ersonally by the representatives must be mailed later lo the Lodges. It IS

The report of the Special Committee to Examine t~e Committee Structure
