Recommendation No. 3-Appointment of Lodge Cha inn en for
Grand Lodge Programs
Many Grand Lodge programs have been developed for the benefit of
constituent Lodges, often at considerable expense to the Grand Lodge and, of
course, to the Lodges in the form of per capita tax. However, all too frequently,
advantage is not taken of these programs by the Lodges because of lack of
appointment of a Brother to serve as Chairman to ensure that these or some
other programs are used.
Grand Lodge Committeemen are often frustrated in their attempts to make
contact with the Lodges because there has been no appointed Chairman for
that activity.
It is believed that the existence of a Chairman in each Lodge will stimulate
further interest in promoting these programs, thus advancing the overall success
of the Lodge.
It is therefore recommended that each Master be required to appoint a
Chairman to correspond with each of the Grand Lodge Standing Committees
listed below:
Public Schools
U.S. Constitution Observance
Masonic Education
Masonic Homes Endowment
This recommendation shall be implemented by adding to Section 2530,
Duties of Master:

.

"7th. To appoint a Chairman in his Lodge to correspond with the Grand
Lodge Committees on Public Schools, U.S. Constitution Observance,
Masonic Education and the Masonic Homes Endowment Board."
Recommendation No. 4-lncreasing Membership on Public Schools Committee
The California Masonic Code Section 1202, Standing Committees,
provides that these Committees shall be appointed by the Grand Master at each
Annual Communication just before the close thereof. Included in these Committees is the Committee on Public Schools, to consist of not less than fifteen
nor more than thirty members.
The adoption of the Drug and Alcohol Abuse Prevention Program in the
Public Schools has placed an added burden on this Committee. There are more
than 540 Lodges and 1,100 school districts in California and the sire of the
Committee is presently limited to 30 members. The average Committeeman
would thus be contacting about 18 Lodges and 37 school districts. In order to
establish and maintain reasonable and effective contact with the Lodges and
schools in all geographical areas of the State, it is necessary to provide additional
members on this Committee. This Committee is also providing manpower to
count and record contributions to the Drug and Alcohol Abuse Prevention
Program.

Differing interpretations of ~s comma~ wor~. make i~ necessary. to

of the ma1ority.

"at any time" and "upon the request...". The sentence would then read as follows:

bis own acnon or upon the request of two-thirds of the Trustees, and
appoint another in the place of the person so removed.".

Recommendation No. 8-Vote Required for Adoption of Legislation
For the adoption of any new legislation or changes in th~ Consti~ut~on and
Ordinances of the Grand Lod&e, it is necessary that a five-sJ.Xths ma1onty v~te
be received (California Masoruc Code Sections 502 and 4002). If a resolu~1on
receives a simple majority vote, it is h71d over untµ the ne~ ~ual Commum~­
tion when it will be reqwred to receive a two-thuds ma1onty vote for adoption
(California Masonic Code Sections 503 and 4003).
The five-sixths majority vote has been debated many times and has been
the subject of resolutions in previous Annual Communications to change these
requirements, but failed to receive the required five-sixths majority vote. S01.ne
other Jurisdictions have adopted a requirement of two-thirds and others reqwre
three-quarters majority vote for adoption of new legislation.
While the five-sixths vote requirement ensures that changes will no~ be

~ad7 pro~scuously, it also penni.ts a small mino~i~ to. d~feat any new legisla-

tion m which a large, but not sufficiently large, ma1onty IS m favor. Base.d Of:l the
average number of ballots cast being 1,400 at recent Annual Commurucat10ns,
the control of any amendment lies in the hands of as few as 234 negative voters.
It has been said th~~~ except for h~usekeeping matters, it is v_ery difficult to ~~e
any changes in Calirornia Masoruc law as long as the five-sJ.Xths rule remains m
force.

~ s a first step, it is believed that a relaxation of the voting requirement from
five-sJ.Xths (83.3 ~ercent) to three-quarters (75 percent) would provide a more
rca~onable but sllll caullous approach to the passage of new legislation. On the
basis .of 1,400 total ballo~s cast, the three-quarters ruJe would require 351
ne&atiye yotcs to defe.at an issue. The carry-over provision requiring a two-thirds
maJonty m the following year should remain in the regulations until the first step
bas been accomplished and tested.

It is therefore my recommendation that Sections 502 and 4002 be amended
to change the words "five-sixths" to "three-quarters".

Recommendation No. J~Fees and Dues Structure
It has become increasingly apparent that the financial status of many
Lodges and Temple Associatio ns is a matter of serious concern. It may also be
the basis for many of o ur present problems with respect to attendance and
membersh ip. In the highly commercia lized and competitiv e environme nt in
which we live, the cost of goods and services has skyrockete d and the demands
for quality have increased. Thus, it is no longer possible to provide for the needs
of our Masonic members at the prices which prevailed not too many years ago.
lo a review of several typical Lodges and Temple Associations, it has been
observed that rents, mortgage payments or buildmg costs have increased by
20-30 times during the past 75 years while Lod~e fees and dues have increased
only about 5 times. In other words, the Fratcrmty' s fees and dues structure has
fallen seriously behind the normal rate of inflation, thus tending to put
Freemason ry in the bargain basement category.
Since this subject is very controvers ial and yet may be one of the root causes
of our current problems, I recommen d that a Special Committee be appointed
by the incoming Grand Master to study the fees and dues structure of the Lodges
and make a report and recommen dations to the Grand Lodge at the next
Annual Communic ation.

Recommendation No. 12-Alcoholic Beverages and Meeting Places

The issue of alcoholic beverages has been the subject of considerable
debate at Annual Communications for many years. Studies have been made,
proposals have been presented and confusion has resulted from a multitude of
separate and S?~etimes ove~lapping Resolutions. This subject has also been
the so~rCC? of fnctton and tension between the Grand Lodge and some affiliated
orgaruzatlons.
The .days of prohibi~on have long passed. Masons in this Jurisdiction now
hold so<.;1al. events at which alcoholic beverages are consumed in places other
than. b~ildings owned or rented by Masoruc organizations. So there is no
res~1ction on l;he ~nsu.mption C?f ~co~olic bevefage~ per se by Masons or
affiliated orgaruzations. The restnct1ons m the Califorrua Masonic Code apply
only to the locations in which alcoholic beverages may be served or consumed.
. Some M~onie related organizations have large investments in buildings
wt;Uch are smtable for conventions or ?anquets at ~hich alcoholic beverages
~ght be served. However, current ~aliforrua Masoruc Code. r.e~lations (Sections 2048 and 2050) do not pernut the rental of such facilities if alcoholic
beverages ~e le_>~ served. Temple Associations have also expressed the need
to rent theu: facilities ~or such events~ w7dding receptions, to help reduce the
burden of high operatmg costs, especially m these times of membership decline.
. ln my travels throughout the ~orld, and from information provided me from
vanous sow:ces, I ~d 11?-at t~e servmg of alcoholic beverages in a building owned
~ya Masomc or~amzat1on IS a genef~Y accepted practice in overseas J urisdicllons. I have witne~ed an~ part1c1pated m the consumption of alcoholic
beverages at Masoruc recephons and banquets in Masonic buildings with due
respect for the first cardinal virtue - T emperance.
~ne of the charges to the Junior Warden of a Lod~e at his installation
reqwres that )01;1 sh?uld practice moderation and discretion in the indulgence
of your own wclinatlons and you should carefully observe that the means of
refreshment are not converted to improper or excessive use".

The t~e has arriv7d to be practical and mature in our approach to the
consumption of alcoholic beverages.

At the 1988 Annual Communicat ion, Resolution No. 88-19 concerning
alcoholic beverages and meeting pla~s r~ceived ~ maj<?rity ~ote ~nd ':Vas carried
over until the 1989 Annual Commurucatton. While this leg1Slat1on, if adopted,
will clarify some of the wording in Sections 2048 and 2050, it does not e;o far
enough in alleviating the confusion surroundin~ this issue. I bclie:ve it is ~till
unnecessaril y restrictive, confus~g and dis~rinunatory. The followmg specific
concerns relate to the proposals m Resolution No. 88-19:
a. The 8th "Whereas" statement of R esolution 88-19 expresses the
belief that "it is probably in the best interest of Craft Masonry to release
control over organization s other than our Craft Lodges and Temple
Associations...and to allow prerequisite organization s to control the_mselves and determine their own regulations ...suhject always to Sectton
2612 of the California Masonic Code which requires all prerequisite
organization s to meet the same standards .of co?d~ct. an? propnety as
are imposed upon all Master Masons of this Jur1Sdict1on . As a general
rule, this approach would be considered reasonable; however, any
suggestion that allows prerequisite organization s to establish th~ir 0\\'.11
regulations but also rcqwres them to conform to the Califorrua
Masonic Code regulations creates an environment for conflict and
misinterpret ation. which is more severe than the condition we now ha:ve.
It is my firm opinion that there can be only one set of standards wh1ch
apply to all Master Masons; any other approach creates a double
standard discriminatio n and a de facto separation within the Fraternity. It ~ preferrable to devise reasonable legislation which is applic.able to all Master Masons equally.
b. The first "Resolved" amendment refers only to Masonic .Lodges and
attempts to restrict the Lodge meetings to places which have a public
entrance separate from a puhlic entrance to prem.ises w~e~ein alcoholic beverages are consumed, served or sold. This restnct1on has
caused endless confusion, especially if such meetings are held in a hotel
or convention center. The requirement for separate entrances is of no
practical significance and should be eliminated.
c. The second "Resolved" amendment also refers only to Masonic
Lodges and allows Lodges to hold social events at which alcoholic
beverages are consumed ... but does not allow those events to be held
"on land or in a building owned, leased or rented by a Masonic Lodge
or Temple Association...". However, the fourth "Resolved" amendment
allows Masonic Lodges to rent their property to tenants for business
or social events wherein alcoholic beverages are consumed ... provided
that the tenant is not a Lodge or prerequisite organization... This
proposal gives the impression that non-Masonic tenants are more
trustworthy than Masonic tenants. It is also hypocritical to deny

The choice of whether alcoholic beverages may be consumed or served in
a Masonic edifice or on property owned by a Masonic organization should be
left to the sound judgment of the individual Lodges, Temple Associations or
Masonic organization s which own buildings used for Masonic purposes under
certain broad guidelines which apply equally to all Masons, regardless of the
organization to which they belong.

It is recommende d that Sections 2048 and 2050 of the California Masonic
Code be repealed and, in their place, the following legislation be adopted:

A Ma~o?ic Lodge or organization the prerequisite of memb~rship
wherem IS that a person be a Master Mason, or TemJ?le Association
may, at its discrellon, permit the serving and consumption of alcoholic
beverages in a building owned or leased by a Masonic organization
provided that no alcoholic beverages may be served or consumed in a
Lodge room or a room in which ceremonies are normally conducted,
except when such room serves a dual purpose as a ceremonial room
and social room.
A Masonic Lodge or organization the prerequisite of membership
wherein is that a person be a Master Mason may hold social events at
which alcoholic beverages arc served, consumed or sold, provided that
no Lodge fund~ arc used to purchase such beverages.
Business meetings of a Masonic Lodge or o rganization the prerequisite
of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason may be
held in a building (e.g. a hotel) in which there is a bar, provided that
no alcoholic beverages are served or consumed at such meeting.
A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association or organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason may
not establish a permanent bar in a building owned or leased by a
Masonic organization .
A Ma~o~c Lodge or organization the prerequisite of membership
wherew 1s that a person be a Master Mason may, directly or through a
Temple Association, rent or lease land or a building in which it has
ownership to business establishmen ts wherein alcoholic beverages are
served, consumed or sold as a minor part of the business.

Recommendation No. JS-Commercial Ventures
Section 2070k of the California Masonic Code states that "Public money
raising schemes should not be indulged in by prerequisite ~odies. lf.they cannot
be supported by their members, they are not worthy of eXJStcnce ....
This langua~e has created some confusion. The Shrine football games f>or
the Crippled Children's Hospitals are public money raising. eve~ts for a char1ty
and are approved activities, according to Section 2070d. Shnne ~cuses are al<>o
public money raising events but the proceeds do not go to a ~hanty. Ii;i the latter
case, tickets must state that the P.~oceeds ~e not for charity and Ucket sales
must be limited to members, families and fnends.
The Masonic youth groups, although not prerequisite. or.ganizations, have
a close alliance with Freemasonry. Yet, there are no restncuons on the youth
groups with respect to solicitation of public support.
In the interest of uniformity, it is believed th~t the sam~ .rules should apply
to all organizations and that, as long as the public fund r~mg event proVJd.es
fair value to the public, it should be permissible. The question of ~he financial
feasibility of the public money raising event is a matter to be determmed by each
organization for the specific event.

It is further recommended that Section II "Public Support" in the Supplement to the California Masonic Code be deleted.

Recommendation No. 16--Gambling
The regulations relating to gambling in the Califoroia Masonic Code are
somewhat confusing in light of changes in State and local laws. Some of the
Annotations to Secuon 3314 and the guidelines in the Appendix cover specific
restrictions which are not relevant to modern society and laws.
To provide broad regulations with respect to gambling, it is sufficient to
simply state that Masons will conform to the laws of the State or community in
which they live. The Lodge or other Masonic organization is therefore responsible for determining what these laws are and controlling their actions accord-

ingly.

DECISION NO. 2
NAMING A LODGE ROOM IN HONOR
OF A .BROTHER MASON
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Grand Master's Decision No.
2 has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has interfreted Section 2002 of the California Masonic
Code precluding the naming o · a Lodge after a living person as not being
applicable to the naming of a building or a room within a building, and fmding
no other Section covering the question, he has decided that it is proper to name
a room or area within a Masoruc Temple in honor of a Brother Mason, whether
living or deceased.
Your Committee fmds that this Decision is consistent with our law and does
not require an Amendment to the California Masonic Code. As a result, only a
majority affirmative vote is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the approval of the
Decision.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

At the 1988 Annual Communication, the Uniform Code of By-Laws _of
Lodges was amended to eliminate the option of paying dues on <I; quai:terly basi;;.
Unfortunately, a conforming amendment was n~t made to ~:1iforma !"fasoruc
Code Section 2692 regarding plural mem~rships ~~ D11D1ts..Section 2692
permits an application for plural membership or a Dlffilt. request if the Brother
mvolved bas paid his dues through the ne~ succ:edmg calendar quarter.
Without the option to pay dues quarterly, this reqwrement no longer ~akes
sense. The Grand Master has therefore ruled that dues need only be paid for
the calendar year in which plural membership or a Dimit is granted.
It is a policy of the Grand Lod§e that our Masonic law be consistef?l and
understandable. The Grand Master s Decision was a reasonable resolution of
an inconsistent and confusing provision.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote
on Grand Master Channon's Decision No. 1.
Decision APPROVED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The Grand Master has ruled that it is proper to name a room or area within
a Masonic Temple in honor of a Brother Mason, whether living or deceased.
The Grand Master was aware of Section 2002 of the California Masonic
Code, which prohibits naming a ~for a living person.
However, there a.re occasions when donations of sizeable amounts of
money can properly be acknowledged by the use of a name. Most Lodges have
a number of rooms and even if the main Lodge room itself is named for a person,
that does not mean that the Lodge itself will bear that name.
The Grand Master made such a distinction and we believe that the distinction is valid.
We, therefore, recommend a "Yes" vote.
Decision APPROVED.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committ ee on Jurisprud ence, to which Grand Master's Decision No.
4 has been referred, reports as follows:
At the 1988 Annual Commun ication, Grand Mascer Mark's Recomm endation No. 6 concerni ng an amendme nt to Section 2602 of the Californi a Masonic
Code, was adopted.
Grand Master Mark had recomme nded that the then present Jaw requiring
the approval of the Grand Master for a Lodge to receive the applicatio n of an
applicant whose physical defects are not correctable with artificial aids be
eliminate d and that the matter be left to the sound discretion and good j udgrnent
of the Lodge. In an attempt to carry out the intent of Grand Master Mark, the

The Committee on Policy and Genera/ Purposes:
. In making the report on G rand Master's Decision No. 4, your Committ ee
wishes to stres~ that we do not question the legitimacy of the degrees conferred
by Chateau Thierry Lodge No. 569.
~s yo.u know, the issue of physical qualification has been a long-stan ding
.
1Ssue m this Grand Lodge dating back over a century.

In ~979, after n~e~ous attemp_ts,_ the Grand Lodge made a significant
c:hange m our law p~rmittmg the admission of candidate s if they could substantially, (rather than literally) conform to our degrees. A part of the legislation

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

adopted in 1979 was the provision which stated, "In the case of defect not
correctable with artificial aids, the application shall not be received by the
Lodge without approval of the Grand Master."

DECISION NO. 5

174

In Grand Master Leo Mark's Recommendation No. 6 in 1988, he recommended that the requirement of the Grand Master's approval be removed from
OUI law, leaving the question "to the sound discretion of the Lodge," but
requiring the Master to "state the nature and extent of his disabilities" before a
ballot was taken. This seems to give a Lodge virtually total discretion. However,
Section 2600, requiring that a candidate be able, with the aid of prosthesis, to
"conform substantially," to the ritual of our degrees was NOT changed by the
adoption of Grand Master Mark's Recommendation No. 6.
Chateau Thierry Lodge No. 569, relying on the amended provisions of
Section 2602, exercised its sound discretion and elected a candidate, a double
amputee, whose condition was not correctable by artificial aids. We must
assume that the candidate was duly notified of his election.
At this point the Ritual Committee requested a decision from the Grand
Master regarding the conferral of degrees on this candidate.
This placed the Grand Master on the horns of a dilemma. If he rigidly
interpreted Section 2600 requiring that a candidate "conform substantially" he
would have had to order the Lodge to reject the candidate, an action which
would have made our Fraternity appear unfeeling and discriminatory. On the
other hand, if he allowed the Lodge to proceed, he would have to modify Section
2600 which states that physical impairment must be correctable at least to the
extent that the candidate can "conform substantially" to the degrees.
While we feel that the Grand Master acted with compassion and understanding in the circumstances presented to him, it should not be the policy of
the Grand Lodge to thus accomplish modifications in our Masonic Code. That
your Grand Master may share our uneasiness on the issue is reflected in his
Recommendation No. 11, which deals with the subject of physical requirements.
If this Grand Lodge wishes to modify Section 2600 to permit conferral of
degrees on candidates who cannot "conform substantially" to our degrees, it
should be done by appropriate legislation. Legislation will be presented to you
later in this session to permit Grand Lodge to act on this question. The
Committee has discussed Recommendation No. 11, and will recommend approval.

However, although we share the Grand Master's sense of compassion
leading to tbis decision, we feel that it was not justified due to the restrictions
of Section 2600.
We stress that disapproval of this decision will not alter the Masonic status
of the candidate.
We, therefore, recommend a "No" vote.
Decision APPROVED.

PROCEED INGS OF THE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Adoption of Grand Master Channon's Recommendation No. 11 would
eliminate all present physical qualification requirements from our law. If
adopted, any man with the physical and mental capacity to learn and practice
the principles of Freemasonry could be made a Mason, regardless of maim or
defect in his body.
Physical qualifications is an emotional issue and has been debated at most
every Annual Communication for over 25 years. Each of us has probably known
a man of good moral character who could have benefitted from Masonic light
and who could have benefitted the Lodge by his contributions as a member that
was denied Masonic membership because of a physical defect. Men have been
rejected by one Lodge but accepted by another because of differing interpretations of our physical requireme nts. We have. debated specific exemptions, such
as for men with hearing aids. We have appointed study groups to consider
reform. Significant reforms were adopted 10 1979. Blind men have since been
made Masons in California. But, there are still physically disabled men who are
barred from Masonry by our current rules, such as the wheelchair bound. The
Grand Master now proposes to take the fmal step: permit admission of anyone
who can "comprehend the significance of the ritual and its application to daily
living". We agree.
When our operative ancestors built the great European cathedrals, physical
prowess was as unportant as moral fitness. The work was hard and dangerous.
A man with a physical maim or defect was of Limited value. From these very
necessary employment requirements developed the doctrine of the perfect
youth: only the man unblemished in mind and body was suitable for Masonic
membership. Masonry took good men, both physically and mentally, and made
them better.
Our Fraternity has not built stone cathedrals for almost 300 years, yet the
physical requirements survive. How relevant are they today? When Masonry
began its transition from operative to speculative, the first men recorded as
adinitted for Masonry's moral and philosophical benefits were British aristocrats who clearly did no physical labor for their livelihood. Today, our
Fraternity sould be a contemplative society, practicing Brotherly love for all
men, demonstrating by our actions in the world the truth which Masonry teaches
about our relationship to God and our fellow man and providing relief for those
who may be at the lowest spoke of life's wheel. Do our current physical
requireme nts have any significance for this vision of today's Masonic mission?
We as Masons are in possession of something timeless, a priceless heritage.
It is our duty to preserve it for those who follow just as our Brothers in years
passed preserved it for us. What are the essences of Freemasonry which are
timeless? Our priceless heritage is our philosof hical and moral teachings.
Ability to do manual labor is not. The doctrine o the perfect youth should be
preserved but only so far as it bars from Masonry those with defects of spirit or
mind which prevent them from learning and practicing our Masonic principles.
It is now time to eomplete our 300 year transition to sr.eculative Masonry by
admitting what has been true since the cathedral building ended: It is the
internal and not the external which makes a Mason.

The California Freemason Publication Board:
The Grand Master's R ecommendation No. 13, which would amend the
California Masonic Code so as to permit advertising in publications of Masonic
Lodges and organizations, the prerequisite wherein is that a r..erson be a Master
Mason, has been referred to the Publication Board of the California Freemason.
Since the Grand Master is the Chairman of the Board, this response is being
made by a member of the Board who is Editor of the California Freemason.
For many years, this Grand Lodge has (and for good reasons at the time)
imposed certain restrictions on the Lodges of this Jurisdiction. We believe the
time has come in this enlightened age for at least one of these prohibitions to
be removed and particularly one which places limitations on freedom of expression.
The Grand Master has proposed that advertising in Masonic and Masonic
related publications be permitted and that Masonry may now go public by
advertising in the news media, a Masonic-sponsored event, the only restrictions
being those of common sense propriety as delineated in the Recommendation.
In the belief that Lodges and Masonic related organizations, given freedom
to manage their own publications, will do so in the best interests of Freemasonry,
the Publication Board recommends a "Yes" vote.

Recommendation HELD OVER.

Special Committee be appointed by the incoming Grand Master to serve as a
liaison and coordinating Committee between the Grand Lodge and appendant
and concordant organi7..ations within the Masonic family.
To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee on
Jwisprudence submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED that the incoming Grand Master be directed to appoint a
Special Committee to be known as the "Masonic Relations Committee" with
duties to include, but not be limited to the following:
a. Serve as a coordinating Committee between the Grand Lodge and
other Masonic organizations with respect to events of common interest.
b. Act as a Liaison Committee for the Grand Master in areas of conflict
between different groups.
c. Promote joint efforts between various Masonic groups in matters of
mutual concern.
Since this Recommendation does not seek to amend the Constitution or
Ordinances, only a majority affirmative vote is required for adoption.

AMENDMENT TO MASONIC TEST OATH
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committe on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 88-6 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to shorten the Masonic Test Oath.
Your Commit~ee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents, except that instead of amending Section 2416 of the California
Masonic Code, only the Monitor is to be amended so that the Resolution will
read:
"NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Test Oath as set
forth in the Monitor be amended to read as follows:
'I,
, in the presence of God and these witnesses, do hereby and hereon, solemnly and sincerely swear: that I am
a Master Mason in good standing. So help me God'".
Since this Resolution, at the last Annual Communication, received less than
the five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority vote, it has
been carried over for reconsideration at this Annual Communication and a
two-thirds affirmative vote is now required for adoption. As a carry-over
Resolution, no further motion for adoption is necessary.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In 1988 your Committee on Policy and General Purposes reviewed the
current test oath and, by comparison of the recommended amendment to the
Officer's Monitor, we found the suggested change to be of significant improvement.

The Committee on Ritual:
The way the printed Resolution is prepar~d, i.t look_s like .only part of one
line of the Test Oath is being changed. Thats IlllSleadmg. Smee many of us
haven't had a reason to hear the Test Oath recently, let me refresh your
memories. The present Test Oath is:
, in the presence of God and these witnesses, do
"I,
hereby and hereon, solemnly and sincerely swear: that I have been
regularly initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason, passed to the degr~e
of Fellow Craft and raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason m
a just and legal manner; that I do nol stand suspended or expelled from
any Lodge of Masons, nor do I know of any reason why I should not
hold Masonic communication with my Brethren. So help me God."

In our estimation, this is an unnecessarily cumbersome way of saying that
you're a Master Mason and entitled to sit in a Lodge. The change we're
suggesting is:
"I

in the presence of God and these witnesses, do

h~reby and hereon, s~lemnly and sincerely swear, that I am a Master

Mason in good standing. So help me God."
What else needs to be said?
We ask your "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed b¥ the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the mtent of the
proponents. However, we call to your attention the fact that the first paragraph
of Section 1102 concerning the withdrawal of funds of the G~and Lodge
provides that the Grand Treasurer alone shall do so unless he IS unable or
unavailable. In that situation, the Grand Master alone or the Deputy Grand
Master and Grand Secretary together may act for him. Thus, should you adopt
this Resolution so as to amend Section 1104, Section 1102 would remam
unchanged with respect to the writing of checks or otherwise withdrawing the
funds of the Grand Lodge.
Since this Resolution, al the last Ann.ual Communication, received less than
the five-sixths vote required f~r adoption, bu~ did receive a major!ty ".ole, it has
been carried over for recons1derahon at this Annual Commumcatlon and a
two-thirds affirmative vote is now reci..uired for adoption. As a carry-over
Resolution, no further motion for adoption is necessary.

The Committee on l'o/icy and General Purposes:
The California Masonic Code does not now provide for the Assistant
Grand Treasurer to act for the Grand Treasurer in his absence or inability. The
Grand Master is authorized to fill in any vacancy in any elective office of the
Grand Lodge, but inability lo act is not defined as a vacancy.
The proponents of this Resolution seek lo correct this deficiency ~y amending Section 1104 of the California Masonic Code ~o add to the dulles of ~e
Assistant Grand Treasurer the requirement to assist the Grand Treasurer m
the discharge of his duties and to act for him in his absence or inability.
The legislation as proposed, accomplishes the dual purpose sought by the
proponents. Your Committee on Policy and General purposes agrees with the
proposed changes and recommends a "Yes" vote.
However, we would caution that the duties of the Grand Treasurer are
enumerated in Section 1104 of the California Masonic Code which is not a part
of this proposal. Therefore, while the Assistant Grand Treasurer would he
authorized to assume the duties of the Grand Treasurer, he would be barred
from withdrawing funds on deposit or bearer securities, sin~ S~ction 1102
specifically names those who can act for the Grand Treasurer m this record.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

All members of the Grand Lodge are potential Committee members. The
pool of eligible and able members is very large.
This Grand Lodge annually increases its membership by the number of
newly elected Junior Wardens, probably over 500.
Experience is helpful, but new members bring new ideas and will soon be
experienced.
More importantly the honor now held by so few for so long should be
shared. So should the hard work.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes the general
purposes of Grand Lodge would be best served by the adoption of this Resolution and recommends a "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The proponent of this Resolution seeks to require ap{lroval of the Committee on Temple Properties for all proposed expenditures m excess of $7,500.00
in respect to the construction, alteration, or improvement of a Masonic Temple.

.

At the 1976 Annual Communication the established limit was adjusted from
$2,500.00 to $5,000.00. Since 1976, inflation exceeds more than 60%. This
Resolution seeks to increase the established threshold by a modest 50% which
the Policy and General Purposes Committee views as fair and reasonable.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee views the proposed increase
as a necessary response to inflation and therefore recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Temple Properties:

Your Committee on Temple Properties feels that this Resolution is a
needed and positive change and gives the Constituent Lodges greater flexibility
in making mmor improvements and at the same time providing for some review
over large expenditures, thereby guarding against financial embarassments. We
strongly recommend a "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The Commitee on Policy and General Purposes:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

233

Resolution No. 88-19 does not, however, permit the use and serving of
alcoholic beverages at Masonic social events on Masonic properties. This is one
of the safeguards many of you have considered to be necessary.
Resolution No. 88-19 is a sophisticated proposal in its construction due to
its definition of the specifics, and yet, contrary to recent proposals, it does not
overstate the issues.
No legislation can be declared perfect until it has been tried and purified
in the "crucible" of time and test. We believe, however, that Resolution No. 88-19
comes closer than anything that has preceded it and deserves the opportunity
to be tried and tested. We recognize its adoption would create an exception to
Section 2612 of the California Masonic Code.
A great number of the delegates at the 1988 Grand Lodge Session agreed
with us as this Resolution fell just percentage points short of the five-sixths vote
required for passage on the first ballot.
We believe that our law should be modified in this area in order to give
greater flexibili~ to all se$ffients of our Fraternity. We further believe that
opportunity has presented itself for us to resolve this issued here today.
We urge a "Yes" vote on Resolution No. 88-19.

The Committee on Taxation:
Because this Resolution prohibits Masonic Lodges and Masonic Temple
Corporations from purchase or consumption of alcoholic beverages, there are
no tax consequences.resulting from adoption of this Resolution.
Rental or lease of Masonic owned property to unrelated tenants engaged
in purchase or other use of alcoholic beverages does not require the landlord
to be a licencee of ABC and no sales tax permit is required. Such rental activitiy
does comply with the Internal Revenue Code 501(c)(2) requirements for
organizations exempt from taxation.

the concerns alluded to. None of them address all

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 89-1 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the ritual in respect to
the lectures in the first and third dewees to require the lecturer to display the
Monitor to the Candidate at those tunes when it is referred to in the lecture.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed b¥ the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the mtent of the
proponents.

This Resolution seeks to amend the Ritual and a five-sixths affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Putposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to require the lecturer in the first
and third degrees to display the Monitor to the Candidate as it is being referred
to in the lecture. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that
the Resolution is unnecessary.
Nothing in the California Masonic Code prevents a Lodge from displaying
the Monitor. Therefore, we feel that the display of the Monitor should be
optional at the discretion of the Lodge.

.

Further, we believe that we should not enact unnecessary legislation to
make mandatory that which presently is permitted. Such legislation tends to
"clutter up" our Masonic Code.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
Throughout our ceremonies, all steps, signs and working tools are either
demonstrated or displayed because they are terms with which the Candidate is
not familiar. Certainly, he cannot be expected to know what a "Monitor" is, al
least in the first dewee. It seems consistent to display one when referring to it.
In fact, it is so log1cal lo do so, we've learned that it is already being done in
many Lodges.
Your Committee on Ritual recommends a "Yes" vote.
Resolution HELD OVER.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudenc e, to which Resolution No. 89-2 bas been
referred, reports as follows:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

241

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes.·
Resolution No. 89-2, if passed, would approve the use, as well as the
possession, of a cipher ritual, but only insofar as the cipher ritual proposed in
the Resolution conforms to the correct California ritual.

The possession of cipher rituals was prohibited by our law until the 1988
session of this Grand Lodge, at which time the regulation prohibiting the
possession of such rituals or ritual books was deleted from our law. However,
no specific cipher was approved for use by California Lodges or their members.
The adoption of the suggested cipher ritual, insofar as it conforms to the
correct California ritual, might well lead to a great deal of confusion. Unless
that cipher ritual were reprinted, with such changes necessitated by our establis hed and adopted ritual, its use could make it extremely difficult for the owners
and users of the cipher to determine what is and what is not in conformity to
our true ritual. Such reprinting is contrary to present Masonic law.
Your Committee bas great concern as to lending Grand Lodge endorsement and support to a commercial venture as would be the case if approval were
granted to the company which publishes and prints the proposed cipher ritual.
For similar reasons the G rand Lodge has not approved or endorsed any
particular organization as a supplier of Fraternal paraphernali a.
The Grand Lodge is entitled to the sole use of its name and insignia which
have been registered with the Secretary of Stale. (See C.M.C. Section 1) If we
authorize a public organization lo use our name and insignia, we are concerned
that some future court action could determine that the Grand Lodge has
relinquished its exclusivity as lo our Fraternal insignia and name. This exclusive
right must be maintaiAed.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:

The proponent of this Resolution seeks to provide for a uniform cipher
ritual for use in California.

Brethren, I'm going to depart from the usual procedure and give you our
recommendation at the beginning of our report. Your Committee on Ritual
recommends a "Yes" vote on this Resolution. Now that I've got your attention,
let me tell you why.

Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the G rand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
porponent.

Last year, the Grand Lodge approved the possession and use of cipher
rituals in this Jurisdiction. T he Resolution which passed, however, did not adopt
or approve any specific cipher; it simply made it legal to have one.

This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative
vote is required for adoption.

This Resolution asks that you adopt a specific cipher ritual for use in
California, but only to the extent that it conforms to the ntual now being taught.
The proponent recognizes that the cipher identified in his Resolution contains
many errors, but wants you to adopt only which is correct, leaving the identification and correction of the errors to the Inspectors and coaches. This is all in
compliance with our present law, and we assume it is what is happening today.

To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolut:Jon.

the preparation room door in the face of the newly obligated .Brother when he
returns for the second section of the degree. Under these circumstances the
Candidate is at all times, in the custody of an officer of the Lodg~. The
proponent ~ncludes that closing the door in this instance may be considered
rude.
How is this circumstance different from the Grand Master's or the
Inspector's Offi~al V~sit? When the GrfiDd Master or Inspector visits, an alarm
is sounded and 10vest1gated. The door. 1s opened to a.ns~er ~he al~~ an~ then
closed while the Master is consulted, before the distmgmsbed V1S1tor is admitted.

If it is appropriate to close the door in the face of the Grand Master or
Inspector, why is 1t rude to do similarly with the Candidate?
We do not believe that there should be a distinction.
It has been a long standing policy of the Grand Lodge to avoid change
unless compelling reasons indicate otherwise. We find none here.

The Committee on Ritual:
From a Candidate's first introduction to Masonic ceremonies, he is left
waiting outside while things happen behind closed doors. In the fust degree, he
bas bad to wait before the Marshal came out to inte.rrogate him. Later, be is told
to wait while permission for him to enter is sought from the Master, and the
door is closed. It's difficult to understand why, only an hour later, he would find
the same procedure objectionable.
One could equally ask why the door is closed in the first section, when the
Candidate can't see anything anyway. The answer, of course, is that permission
to enter is being formally asked from the presiding officer. Tb.at formality
dictates that it be requested and answered privately. Although we know of no
instance in which it has happended, circumstances might demand that the
Master deny the Candidate's reentry. Suppose, for example, that an objection
had just been raised.
The proponent correctly points out that the Lodge contains nothin~ the
Candidate is not entitled to see. We feel, though, that the element of surprise is
intportant; that the newness of the first impression is diminished if the Candidate is allowed to study the Lodge room during the time the Senior Deacon
is requesting permission. Also, in each case the Master instructs the Senior
Deacon what 1s next to be done with the Candidate. If the Candidate is made
aware of what's going to happen, it interrupts the gradual evolution of the
second section of a degree.
We feel this Re'solution addresses a problem which doesn't exist, and
proposes a solution with more potential for harm than good. The Committee
on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

249

The proponents of this R esolution seek to change the California Masonic
Code to provide for the appointment of Lodge Lecturers and to delete the
requirement for the Master, Senior Warden, and the Junior Warden to qualify
in the Lectures of the Degrees which are delivered from the Master's station.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

We conferred with Ritual and felt their proposal meets three of the four
criteria. However, we feel the issue of the word is a matter of continuing
concern.

WHEREAS, many Lodges are having difficulty getting members to go
through the Officer's line, particularly the offices of the WarC:lens and Master,
due to the reluctance. of members to devote the time and effort necessary to
qualify in the Lectures of the Degrees. Many who start, drop out before reaching
the Elective Offices; and

Another concern of the Policy and General Purposes Committee is that the
abbreviated form of closing would become the practice rather than the exception and the full form closing would rarely be used.

WHEREAS, the o~ratioo of the Lodge may be logically divided into three
sections: (a) the Administration of the Lodge, (b) the Conferral of Degrees and
(c) the Lecture explaning the Degree; and

We also note that the net saving of time would be negligible, amounting to
only a few minutes at most. In view of such insignificant benefit, it does not
warrant such a change. We, therefore, recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
Every time the Grand Lodge is opened for one of its ceremonies around
the State, and the Grand Master exercises his prerogative to use a short form
closing, we are asked why such a closing is not avaiJable to the Constituent
Lodges. Our answer, of course, is that it is important for a Candidate to see and
hear the entire degree, including the closing.
There are occasions, though, on which a shortened closing ceremony would
be practical. Some examples are, when a Lodge is ope.oed for proficiency
examination or, following the annual Installation of Officers or, after a funeral.
No one profits by having to sit through a formal closing in one of these situations.
On the contrary, the full closing ceremony is viewed as an annoying necessity.

WHEREAS, while many members are willing and capable of performing
all three functions, some are effective at administration, but are not necessarily
good Lecturers. Others are more talented at Lecturing, but for various reasons,
cannot or are not willing to devote the time and effort to the administrative
duties and the practices necessary for correct Degree conferral; and
WHEREAS, that in order to reduce the workload burden on the Master
and the Wardens, that they be encouraged, but not required to qualify in the
Lectures of the Degrees which are delivered from the Master's station. That an
Appointive Office of Lecturer be created and that no less than two members
be qualified and certified by the District Inspector for the Lectures in each of
the Degrees.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 89-8 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the California Masonic
Code to provide for the appointment of Lodge Lecturers and to delete the
requirement for the Master, Senior Warden and Junion Warden to qualify in
the Lectures of the Degrees which are delivered from the Master's station.
Your Committee fmds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend the 0 rdinances and a five-sixths affirmative
vote is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution would provide for the appointment of at least two Lodge
Lecturers in each Lodge and would eliminate the requirement that Masters and
Wardens qualify in the Lectures of the Degrees. They would still give the
remainder of the degree work.

.

The proponent feels that, by lessening the work load, that more Brothers
can be attracted into leadership in our Lodges, and those who are too busy lo
learn the lecturers would provide leadership for the Lodges.
To ascertain as to whether or not this might work successfully we might take
a look where something similar has been tried. In 1968, the Grand Commandery
of Knights Templar of the State of California passed legislation authorizing
officers to serve if they were proficient in the opening, closing and conduct of
business, with the orders to be conferred by select teams at a Commandery or
district level. For a few years there was an adequate supply of people to man
these teams. Today it is a rarity to find a Commandery that can do the work.
The reservoir of people who had learned the work has dried up, and no one is
stepping forward to replace them.
·
The argument used to support this change in Commandery is similar to
those used to support this Resolution, that more people will take leadership
roles if it is made easier. Brethren, it did not happen in Commandery.
The title of Past Master has a certain and definite meaning, so much so that
it has found its way into our standard dictionaries. Funk and W agnalls defines
the term of Past Master as "one who has a thorough experience. in something".
~fas?nically, a "thorough experience" most certainly would involve the qualification m the lectures.

Basically, we feel that the experience of the other~ can give us good_ r~ason
to be skeptical of possible benefit, and lacking such eVJdence of benefit it IS not
our policy to make changes.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee onJ urisprudence, to which Resolution No. 89-11 has been

The proponents of this Resolution seek to authorize an apron for an
installed Master to wear when seated on the sidelines of his Lodge.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative
vote is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolubon.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution proposes to have a special apron for the Worshipful Master
to wear when in the Lodge room, but not presiding. The proponents point out,
that if not a Past Master, he is then required to wear a plain white apron while
sitting on the sidelines.
The white apron is an emblem of innocence and the badge of a Mason.
There is nothing demeaning in wearing a plain white apron. Is there some
compelling need for those in the Lodge room to identify the installed Master
on those occasions when be is in the Lodge room, but not in the East? Quite
frequently, the Worshipful Master sits in the South while the Junior Warden
confers th~ first degree. While doing so he wears ~he aP,ron of that station. There
are other mstances when the Master wears a plam white apron, at funerals, for
example, and does so even if serving as Master. This does not seem to cause
confusion in the Temple.
Furthermore, we know of no prohibition against the Worshipful Master
wearing a Master's apron anytime when he is in the Lodge room even if not
residing or filling another station. U a Lodge wishes to purchase an additional
apron for him to wear at such times, it is apparently permissible.

259

In 1980 in Resolution No. 80-4, a proposal was made to permit former
Inspectors to continue to wear their Inspectors' aprons after they ceased to
se!"e, to grant them recognition for their service to the Fraternity. This was
rejected by Grand Lodge on the basis that it would lead to a multiplicity of
aprons. The authorized aprons in this Grand Lodge are: the distinctive Past
Gra!ld Master's apron, the apron of a Gr~d L_odge Officer or lnspe.ctor while
servmg, the Lodge Officer aprons, the plam white aprons, and, long established
custom, the Past Master's apron. It should remain so. We recommend a "No"
vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
The badge of a Mason is a white apron. There is none finer, nor one which
should be accorded more respect. lndeed, many Lodges use notbin~ but white
aprons. In others, all offices' aprons are identical, with no special insignia. Even
in Lodges with special officers' aprons, only one officer should be represented
as the Master.
We might add that we don't know what a Master's apron would look like if
the Master's emblem was removed; what would be left?
Additionally, the purchase of an additional apron could be a financial
burden on some Lodges.
Your Committee on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:

First, my Brethren, we must tell you that we are grieved to learn that any of
you has so little confidence in the Masonic integrity of the Ritual Committee to
honestly believe that we could have acted in a manner which could be labeled
"arbitrary", "capricious" or "whimsical". We h.ave two prim~ry goals; to m~e the
performance of our work as clear and me~gful as possible to the Ci:ln~1d~te,
and to insure that the work is presented uniformly throughout our Junsd1ct1on.
Any change we make is intended to accomplish those goals. We know th~t any
change, no matter how minor, is unsettling, so none - not one - is made wtthout
due deliberation and discussion (sometimes debate) among the members of our
Committee. Let me assure you, no change is made as a "caprice" or "whim".
I have personally spoken to many of you regarding the new location for the
candidate's chair. I've found that the cause for your upset is often not the change
itself, but that the reasons f<;>r the change have ~een faultily e~Lained to you,
or, in some cases, not explamed at all. If I was 10 your place I d be mad, too.
Perhaps, if you know our rationale, you'll agree that the changes are appropriate
and enhance the effect of our ceremonies.
(REASONS INVOLVE ESOTERIC MATERIAL AND
WILL BE EXPLAINED BUT CANNOT BE PRINTED)
The effect of this Resolution, however, goes beyond the change in the
location of the chair. It would prevent any change in floor work or the positionin~ of Officers or Candidates. My Brethren, the members of the Ritual Committee must be allowed certain discretionary latitude in adapting the ritual to
meet specific c-0nditions. Lodges come in all shapes, sizes and configurations.
There are, for example, Lodges in which one or both of the entry doors are in
the North wall. We must make on-the-spot decisions as to how the ritual must
be changed to accomodate unusual conditions. This Resolution would deny us
that right.

YOUTH GROUPS - PUBLIC CEREMONI ES
(89-13)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the provisions of the
California Masonic Code providing for exemplification by Masonic sponsored
Youth Groups of their ritualistic work at Lodge meetings.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

WHEREAS, the youth of any society is its life blood who, with proper
training and support, will assure that society's continued vitality; and
WHEREAS, Masonic sponsored youth groups have, as its founders, members of the Masonic family; and
WHEREAS, Annotations "o" and "p" to Section 2316 of the California
Masonic Code permit Lodges, by Resolutton, to sponsor specific Masonic youth
groups; and
WHEREAS, the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California has further
established a Special Committee on Youth Orders to promote effective Fraternal relations wtth specific Masonic youth groups, promote youth programs in
the Lodges, and encourage Lodge members to provide adult leadership to local
youth groups; and
. WHEl_lEAS, Ma<;onic sponsored youth groups, as described in the Califorrua. Masoruc Code, encompass the same common philosophies regarding a
belief in God and a 'future existence and embraced all religions without discrimination as to religious affiliation or denomination; and

Outdoor degrees seem to be becoming more popular. In every one of these
degrees, adaptations of the ritual must be made to fit the circumstances. This
Resolution would make that impossible.

WHEREAS, under the regulations governing organizations subject to the
jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of California, the Masonic family includes all prerequisite and concordant bodies, including Masonic sponsored youth groups as described in California Masonic Code Section 2316, Annotations "o" and "p"; and

Each Lodge now has the right to decide questions of physical qualifications.
The Ritual Committee must decide how the ritual must be changed to deal with
various handicaps. This Resolution would prevent us from doing so, so we have
a Catch-22. The Lodge has elected a Candidate who cannot receive the degree
in the usual form, but no one has the right to adapt the ritual so that he can
receive a degree.

WHEREAS, nothing in the California Masonic Code prohibits a constituent Masonic Lodge from inviting members of Masonic sponsored youth
groups to attend and/or participate in any public Masonic event, including open
Installations of Officers; and

The men elected and appointed to the Ritual Committee are dedicated to
the faithful performance of tile degrees and no one takes his responsibility more
conscientiously. They are selected for their knowledge of the ritual and confidence in therr integrity as men and as Masons. This Resolution would invalidate that confidence and impose shackles which would deny them the
discretionary latitude necessary to perform the duties of their offices. We ask
your "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

~en continually, encouraged by the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Califor-

W~REAS? it is kn<?wn that the .rules of membership and adopted

WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code does not provide sufficient
direction relative to the involvement of Masonic recognized and/or supported
youth groups at open Masonic events, such as Installation of Officers; and
WHEREAS, there is a perceived confusion relative to the provisions of the
California Masonic Code as it pertains to the degree of involvement of Masonic
sponsored youth groups at Masonic events, particularly the Installation of
Officers which are open to all members of the public without regard to religious
affiliation or denommation.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the California Masonic
Code be amended by adding thereto Section 2317 to read as follows:
Section 2317. A Lodge, by Resolution, may sponsor an Assembly or
Assemblies of the International Order of Rainbow for Girls, a Bethel
or Bethels of the International Order of Job's Daughters, or a Chapter
or Chapters of the International Order of DeMolay. A Lodge may
invite any Assembly, Bethel, or Chapter of such Masonic sponsored
youth groups to exemplify, before the Lodge, at any public meeting, all
or any portion of the ritualistic work of such youth group.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Annotations "o" and "p" to Section
2316 be repealed.

presented and considered at any time upon consent of five-sixths vote
of the members present. All such Resolution s and recommen dations
shall be referred to the Committee on Jurisprude nce which shall report
thereon before a vote is taken. When the report to said Committee is
presented, the vote shall be taken on the amendmen t.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprude nce, to which Resolution No. 89-14 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponent of this R esolution seeks to require that reports of Committees of this Grand Lodge on the Resolution s to be considered at an Annual
Communic ation be distnbuted at the same time that the Resolution s themselves
arc distributed .
Your Committee finds that the legislaiton as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituen t Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponent .

This Resolution seeks to amend the Constitutio n and Ordinance s and a
five-sixths affirmative vote is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In essence, this Resolution would have the several Committee s which arc
to make reports o n most matters coming before the Grand Lodge make those
reports in writing at least ninety (90) days before the Annual Communic ation
and the Grand Secretary transmit both the Resolution s and the reports to
Lodges sixty ( 60) days before the Communic ation.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

269

ll is true that there are technicalities which cause withdrawa l or rejection
of some Resolutions. Some o f these are discoverab le before the Annual Communication ; some are not. H owever, there is nothing in this Resolution which
provides a remedy for such_ technical ~efects. Defective Resolutions could not
be amended on the floor without causmg new problems.
It is also true that some Resolution s are d efeated due to Committee
comments presented for th e first time immediately prior to the ballot.
We do not say that could not be changed, but let us explain present Policy
Committee procedure . After the Jurisprude nce Committee has revised the
propos.ed Resolution s, they are submitted to the Policy and General Purposes
Committe e and to Masters of Lodges and others.
The Policy ComnUltee does not meet until the Friday before the Annual
Communic ation. The Committee is po lled and writing assignmen ts are made,
and drafts of r eports are prepared before we meet. The Committee commence s
it's meetings on the Friday preceding the Annual Communic ation. Very often
we have questions. Many o f t hose are answered when proponent s or ot hers
appear in the Committee room. Such advice could not be available if w e met
earlier.
The final reports are often not prepared until M onday or even Tuesday,
the d ay they are usually presented.
Most polic~ consider~tions arc not expressly set forth in our Co_de. Fo r. t his
reaso n, the Policy Commtttee bas often been called a G reat Debating Society.
We often argue ~orously, making all the points we can think of on each side.
Once we have decided, we present the arguments that persuaded us.

.

If the proposed change were made, sufficient time would need to be given

to allow these debates to occur. We believe it would require two weekend
sessions. The cost would likely be between $8,000.00 and $10,000.00. The same
Committe e members would still need to attend the Annual Communic ation and
the cost of that would be less than our present five-day expense but would
probably be $5,000.00. Other Committee s would have similar problems and
additional expenses.
At the present time the Committee on Distributio n assigns proposals to
Committee s. U nder this Resolution, that power would be given to the G r and
Secretary.
The benefit would be to allow members of Grand Lodge to know the
opinions of the several Committee s at an earljer time. But there is no provisio n
for amendmen t of defective proposals. Thus, the benefit might be to allow the
preparatio n of rebuttal arguments in a few cases.
We do no t believe that minor benefit to be worth the added cost.
We recommen d a "No" vole.

Relative to Resolution No. 89-14, the Committee on Finance feels that the

the Resolutions, prepare the reports and make their recommendat10ns. This

Your Finance Committee is of the opinion that funds required to finance
this Resolution will be excessive and recommends a "No" vote.

GRAND ORATION
"NOBODY SAID IT WOULD BE EASY"
Lee A. Strong, Grand Orator

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Before I begin there are two things I would like to do.
First I want to express my thanks to the Grand Master for giving me the
opportunity to serve this year as Grand Orator . It has been a rich and rewarding
experience to be a part of this Grand Family and to be able to travel throughout
the State and see first hand, Masonry in action in the local Lodges. We may have
problems but it is refreshing to see the optimism and enthusiasm which are
abundant among the members of this Grand Jurisdiction. The other members

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

271

of this Grand Family have also asked me to express the admiration, respect and
affection we have for our Grand Master. Most Worshipful, you have truly been
an inspiration.
The second thing I feel I must do, is to make the following disclaimer.
"The views expressed in this Grand Oration are my own and do not
necessarily represent those of the Grand Master, the Grand Lodge Officers,
the members of this Grand Lodge or the members of the various Constituent
Lodges."
Why do I feel it necessary to say this?
The California Masonic Code states, in part, "It shall be the duty of the
Grand Orator, at each Annual Communication, to deliver an address to the
9r~d. lfldg~ upon matters apper.t~ng to. the Craft ...". ~ believ~ there is
unplic1t m this charge, the responsibility to dJScuss those things which are of
concern and of importance to the Craft. This discussion should identify these
problems, review some of the causes and effects and point out and evaluate
possible solutions. Since my remarks are necessarily subjective and contain
personal biases I offer the preceding disclaimer.
I also expect that there will be disagreement with some of the things I am
going to say. If there were not, this would be a pretty bland talk. Disagreement
IS good if 1t generates dialogue and discussion. Dialogue and discussion are
beneficial if they generate positive action. My hope is that this Grand Oration
will stimulate further discussion between you and your Lodge members. I
especially hope that these discussions will motivate you and your members to
consider positive and.forceful steps to deal with the issues or problems which
are of concern to your Lodge.
Let me tell you a story about motivation. I first heard this in this Grand
Lodge in 1969 when it was told by the Grand Chaplain, Dr. Kenneth A. Carlson.
It is about a young man who was walking through a cemetery late one night when
he accidently tripped and fell into an open grave. He struggled for a while and
tried to get out but he just couldn't qmte make it. He finatly decided to settle
down and spend the rught. About fifteen minutes later another young fellow
came along m the same cemetery. He tripped and fell into the same grave. He
struggled for about ten minutes, but he could not get out. Finally he decided
he'd better settle down and hoped someone would find him in the morning. He
was just on the verge of getting comfortable when a hand reached out in the
dark, tapped him on the shoulder and a voice said, "You can't get out of here."
But he did!!
Fear is, perhaps the greatest motivator of all. There are however, other
more practical and effective forms of motivation.
In this story the two young men were faced with the same problem. How to
get out of a grave into which they had inadvertently fallen. One of them was
successful because he was more strongly motivated than the other.

272

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

Our Lodges are faced with what mi~t be considered a struggle to climb
out of an abyss of declining membership. As a matter of fact, virtuafiY every issue
considered at this and recent Annual Communicat ions has attempted to deal
with this problem. I hope we can find the motivation to work our way out of this
hole in which we seem to have fallen.
Let me discuss with you some concerns I have about what I have been
hearing relative to suggested causes and proposed solutions for declining
membership . Then I will talk about some steps we might take in our Lodges and
at Grand Lodge to deal with this problem.
I am concerned when I hear that Grand Lodge must bear much of the
responsibilit y for our loss of members and that Grand Lodge must find ways to
turn things around. There is no question that Masonic Law and Custom can
have an inhibiting effect on our efforts to get more members. There is no doubt
that things might be easier if some of the rules could be changed. But even if
this happens, and maybe it has, it docs not mean that you can go home and wait
for applicants to come to your door. Grand Lodge programs can promote
Freemasonry statewide but new members are the resillt of the efforts of the
individual members of individual Lodges.
I am concerned when I hear that people don't know who we are, what we
do or what we stand for. I am concerned because I think this is true. And it is
true because we don't talk about Freemasonry .
Think back to the time you applied for membership in your Lodge. Remember when members of the Investigating Committee came to your home and
talked to you and your wife and family. Remember how interested your friends
and associates were in what you were doing. Theo remember the night you got
your First Degree. The experience was almost overwhelmin g. The solemnity of
the occasion, the ancient uses and customs, the sheer volume of information.
Most of all, you remember you were told that part of the work was secret and
must never be revealed. Since you had no idea what was secret and what was
not, it was easier and safer to say nothing. Family, friends and associates who
were interested were rebuffed and soon lost interest. ln addition, the fact that
we don't solicit members, made you even more cautious. And that is the way
you have been ever since. That is the way we all are.
I think there are other reasons we are not very good at talking abo ut
Freemasonry . I think we are afraid someone will ask us a question we can't
answer. Questions about Ritual and Masonic secrets. Other questions like: How
did Masonry start? What do you get out of Masonry? What will I get out of
Masonry? What is the difference between you and the Elks or the Odd Fellows?
Why do you wear those funny aprons? And the toughest one of all. What do
Masons do?
I also think we are reluctant to talk about Freemasonry because it is
sometimes hard to tell another person why we really love this Fraternity. It is
difficult to put into words the relationship that exists among our members. We
strul1Jde to describe the harmony we feel in a Masonic Lodge. We can discuss
it wiili each other but not with outsiders. In today's society, brotherly love is
easily misundersto od.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

273

I am concerned because we seem to have a tendency to look for easy

~wers for a difficult problem. We hear that there is too much emphasis on

Ritual. Our Lectures are too long. We need to shorten the closing ceremonies.
Our Candidates have too much lo learn. A Cipher Ritual is the ariswer. We need
to make it easier to get men to serve as officers. Grand Lodge wi.11 have to get
in touch with the times.
One fallacy with this approach is the presumption that these practices and
policies somehow negatively influence. a person's decision to become a member
of a Masonic Lodge. We might argue that these procedures have an adverse
effect on Lodge attendance or on the willingness of members to serve as officers
or coaches. However, the prospective applicant can be little influenced by those
things of which he has only scant, if any, knowledge.
I am_concerned when I hear that we don't have enough time. We don't have
enough t101e to teach all of the Ritual. We don't have enough time to give the
complete Lecture or to close Lodge properly. Our Candidates are too busy to
learn the Lectures in their entirety.
Let me tell you about Masonry in Whittier twenty-five or thirty years ago.
Now I know, there is nothing more boring than hearing how it was in the good
old days, particularly from some senior citi7..en who has probably lost touch with
reality. But please humor me.
Back in the late Fifties and early Sixties we had no shorta~e of Candidates.
ln 1957, when I applied for membership in Greenleaf Lodge, 11 took more than
a year to get all the Degrees. As a matter of fact, in that year the Lodge Raised
~ M~ster Masons i~ addition to conferring all the other Degrees. This same
situation was found m most of our Lodges. Thin~ finally started to slow down
b~t for many years w~ still complained that we did not have enough time to do
thmgs prope~ly. Oh, we fou_nd time.to <;o~er all the Degrees in thei_r entirety
~d the Candidates gave their Profic1enc1es m full form. But what we didn't have
tim.e J~r, was to tal.k about Freemasonry . We did not have time for family
acllVJhes. We were unable to plan interesting and informative meetings. We
often said that when the Degree work slowed down, we would correct these
deficiencies. Now the work has slowed and still wc are told, "we don't have time".
. Finall~, I am concerned that in our efforts to get more members we might
Wind up with less Mason.ry. If we make it easier to get Candidates and if we
shorten the D egrees and if we reduce requirements for advancemen t then when
do we teach Masonry? And who will be the teachers? Yes we do need members
'
but in the process let's not forget what originally got us here.
Last year the Grand Orator, the Worshipful Charles H. Alexander
delivered .an insp~ed Oration in which he suggested that we "stop worrying
about gettmg men mto Masonry and concentrate on getting Masonry into Men",
He also d_eclared, "our jo~ is to keep the principles of Masonry alive, not to
compromise them away in a futile attempt to make this institution more
popular". He had much more to say and it was enthusiastica lly received by the
members of Grand Lodge. I mention his talk because I share his views and I
WaD;t to expand upon his theme.

I think we can get more Masonry into men and I think we can get more men
into Masonry. But it is going to take more time, not less. It will require planning
and dedication at the Lodge level. It necessitates turning sideliners mto ~~k
ticipants. I know you have heard this before. I know you are skeptical. But l ·
about how much fun it would be. And think about the rewards.
The greatest potential salesman for Freemasonry is our newest member.
He has taken the big step. He is ready and willing to learn. He will be an
enthusiastic voice if we give him the information and don't scare him into silence.
When a Candidate first crosses the threshold of a Masonic Lodge, he
should be received as someone very special. He represents the future of
Masonry, he is the reason we are here. His Degrees should be conferred with
dignity, restraint and veneration. He only gets them once. And we certainly have
the time to do them well.
Candidates Coaches should be accessible and other Lodge members
should be available to answer questions and further the new member's
knowledge of Freemasonry. Over the last six or seven hundred years, Master
Masons have been teaching Entered Apprentices many of the same things we
teach today. Doesn't that excite you just a little bit? I think it will stimulate your
pupil. Yes, I know you've heard this before. And maybe you are skeptical, but
again, think about the rewards. And we do have the time.
We need to do a better job of talking about Freemasonry. We need to talk
about what people want to hear. We need to be positive and upbeat. You can't
sell negatives. People are not interested in our problems. They have plenty of
their own. So what are some of the positive things we can say?
Well, we are the oldest and largest, and yes, the most respected Fraternal
organization in the world. We are also the most unique. We do not trace our
history to a particular place or a Sf><:Cific person nor to an exact time. We don't
really know too much about our ongins, but we do know that we are descendants
of builders. Builders with superior skill who, among other things, designed and
erected many magnificent Cathedrals, some of which still remain standing in
Europe and En~and today. These operative Masons assembled in Lodges or
Guilds and tau t their building skills and secrets to others who would carry on
their great wor . In this process they taught, not only how to build buildings of
outstanding beauty, but how to build men of character and integrity.
From these humble beginnings, these Lodges or Guilds evolved into today's
Speculative Lodges where men continue to build character and integrity and
where we practice brotherly love, relief and truth. Our Masonic Lodges represent an oasis where men gather to refresh their spirits, away from the grinding
activities of our everyday existence. Our Lodges are places where brotherly love
really exists, where men truly care about one another and where family is
preeminent.
We are proud of our long list of distinguished leaders. Patriots, Presidents,
writers, and philosophers have taken our vows and ~aced our Lodges. To recite
the history of our older Lodges is to recount the history of the communities in
which they are located. Many of today's local, state and national leaders are
members of Masonic Lodges and we should publicly acknowledge them.
